m1-l1.html:
What you'll learn

  • Choose between the Scratch online editor and the Scratch app, and know what each one gives up.
  • Open Scratch on your own device and pass a one-block test.
  • Decide, together with a parent or guardian, whether to make a Scratch account.
  • Fix the setup problems that stop most beginners on day one.

Every game in this course gets built in one free program: Scratch 3, made by the Scratch Foundation. That includes a race with a fair start, a crab that catches falling starfish, a platformer with gravity, and a multi-level game of your own. Most people never install anything. You open a web page, and an orange cat sits on a white stage waiting for instructions.

This lesson gets you to that cat on whatever computer you have, and makes sure your setup will still work next week.

#What you need

Thing Details
A computer with a keyboard Windows 10 or newer, a Mac with macOS 10.13 or newer, a Chromebook, or a Linux computer
A current web browser Chrome, Firefox, Edge, or Safari. Scratch won't run in Internet Explorer.
A mouse or trackpad A mouse makes dragging blocks easier, but a trackpad works
Speakers or headphones Sound matters from Module 4 on
Money None. Scratch and everything in this course is free.

Scratch also runs on Android tablets and iPads, but the games here are steered with arrow keys and the space bar, so plan on using something with a real keyboard. The Scratch app for Android works on tablets only, not phones.

#Two ways to run Scratch

There are two versions, and they make the same projects. A file you make in one opens in the other.

Online editor Scratch app
Where it lives A web page at scratch.mit.edu A program installed on your computer
Needs internet? Yes, while you work No, once it's installed
Where projects are saved In your Scratch account, or as a file you download As a file on your computer (inside the app on Chromebooks)
Sharing with others A Share button, if you have an account Upload the file on the website first (the Chromebook app can share directly)
Best for Almost everyone, including school computers Spotty internet, or computers where websites are blocked

#Option 1: The online editor, on any device

  1. Open your browser and go to scratch.mit.edu.
  2. Click Create in the blue bar at the top of the page. You can also go straight to scratch.mit.edu/projects/editor.
  3. The editor opens with the cat in the middle of the stage. If a tutorial window pops up, close it with the X.
  4. Bookmark the editor page so you can get back in one click.

That's the whole install. You don't need an account to build, run, or save projects this way.

#Option 2: The Scratch app

Pick your system. The download page at scratch.mit.edu/download usually detects it for you.

Windows

  1. Go to scratch.mit.edu/download. If it shows a different system, choose Windows.
  2. Click the Microsoft Store badge, then Get or Install in the Store. Scratch has switched off its direct Windows download at times, so the Store is the dependable route.
  3. When it finishes, open the Start menu, type Scratch, and click the Scratch app.
  4. If the Microsoft Store is blocked on a school laptop, use the online editor instead. It does everything this course needs.

macOS

  1. Go to scratch.mit.edu/download and choose macOS if it isn't already selected.
  2. Either click the Mac App Store badge and install from there, or click Direct download to get a .dmg file.
  3. If you downloaded the .dmg, double-click it and drag Scratch 3 into your Applications folder.
  4. Open Scratch 3 from Applications or Launchpad. The first time, macOS may warn that the app came from the internet and ask if you want to open it. Click Open.

Chromebook

  1. Go to scratch.mit.edu/download on the Chromebook and click the Google Play badge. It opens the Scratch app's page in the Play Store.
  2. Click Install, then open Scratch from the launcher.
  3. The app keeps projects inside itself. To get a project out as a file, open the three-dot menu on the project, choose Share, then export and pick Google Drive, Files, or email.
  4. School Chromebooks often hide the Play Store. If yours does, use the online editor in Chrome. It runs well there.

Linux

There is no official Scratch app for Linux. Use the online editor in Chrome or Firefox. Every lesson in this course works there.

#Account or no account?

Talk this one over with a parent or guardian. You can finish the entire course without an account by saving project files to your computer. An account adds a few conveniences:

  • Save now in the File menu saves to your account, and Scratch also saves on its own every so often while you're signed in.
  • My Stuff lists every project you've made, on any computer you sign in from.
  • The Backpack lets you carry scripts and sprites from one project to another.
  • You can share projects, comment, and remix other people's work.

If you decide to join, click Join Scratch at the top of scratch.mit.edu. Scratch warns you not to use any part of your real name in your username, and it means it. If you're under the age Scratch uses for your country, it asks for a parent's email address, and a parent has to confirm the account before you can share or comment. In some countries the parent's permission comes before you can use the account at all.

#The one-block test

Whichever option you chose, prove it works:

  1. Click the blue Motion circle on the far left.
  2. Drag the move (10) steps block into the big empty area in the middle.
  3. Click the block once.

The cat should slide a little to the right. Below the stage you'll see boxes labeled x and y. Watch the x box as you click:

A new project always puts the cat at x 0, y 0, the exact center of the stage. Each click adds 10 to x. If your numbers change like this, Scratch is ready.

💡 Tip

Dragged a block somewhere you didn't mean to? Drag it back onto the block palette on the left and it disappears.

#If something goes wrong

"Browser is not supported," or a gray, empty page. Scratch shows that message in browsers it can't run in. Update your browser, or switch to an up-to-date Chrome, Firefox, Edge, or Safari. If the page stays blank, try a private or incognito window; a browser extension may be getting in the way.

The editor is slow or jumpy. Close other tabs, especially ones playing video. The stage-size buttons above the top-right corner of the stage include a small-stage mode, which shrinks the stage and gives the code area more room. On an older computer, the Scratch app often runs smoother than the website.

No sound. Check the computer's volume first. Then check that the browser tab isn't muted: in Chrome, right-click the tab and look for Unmute site. To test, click the Sounds tab above the blocks and press the play button on the cat's Meow sound.

The school network blocks scratch.mit.edu. Ask your teacher or the school's tech staff to allow it, and use the Scratch app at home in the meantime.

#Further reading

  • Download the Scratch app (opens in a new tab): the official install page, with the requirements for each system and an FAQ for the app.
  • Scratch for parents (opens in a new tab): what Scratch is, how the online community is moderated, and answers to common parent questions.
  • Scratch Community Guidelines (opens in a new tab): the rules everyone agrees to before sharing or commenting.

m1-l2.html:
What you'll learn

  • Find the menu bar, block palette, code area, stage, and sprite pane in the Scratch editor.
  • Build four small scripts, each testing one part of your setup.
  • Save a project, start a new one, and load your file back.
  • Know which test to rerun when something stops working later.

Picture yourself in Module 4. Your crab won't follow the mouse, your music is silent, and you've stared at the same script for twenty minutes. Is the code wrong, or is something about the computer itself off? Ten minutes spent now on a test project answers that question for good.

So your first project is a systems check: four tiny scripts that each test one piece of your setup, plus one test for saving. When something breaks later, you can open this project and know in a minute whether the problem is your code or your computer.

#A map of the editor

Open the editor (from the last lesson) and find each of these. The video at the end of this lesson shows them in motion.

  1. The menu bar, across the top. File holds saving and loading. Edit holds Restore and Turbo Mode. Tutorials opens Scratch's own guides, and Debug opens a deck of tips for getting unstuck. The gear-shaped Settings menu changes the language and the color mode.
  2. The tabs, just below the menu bar on the left: Code, Costumes, and Sounds. They show the code, pictures, or sounds of whichever sprite is selected.
  3. The block palette, down the left side. The colored circles are categories: Motion, Looks, Sound, Events, Control, Sensing, Operators, Variables, and My Blocks. Clicking a circle scrolls to those blocks. The button at the very bottom adds extensions like Pen and Music.
  4. The code area, the big space in the middle. You drag blocks here and snap them into scripts. The +, −, and = buttons in its bottom-right corner zoom in, zoom out, and reset.
  5. The stage, top right, where your project runs. The green flag starts it and the red stop sign stops everything.
  6. The sprite pane, under the stage. It lists your sprites and shows the selected sprite's name, x, y, size, direction, and whether it's visible.
  7. The Stage panel, on the far right of the sprite pane, where you pick backdrops. The Stage can have scripts too.

#What each test proves

#Test 1: The green flag

Make sure the cat (Sprite1) is selected in the sprite pane. Find each block by its color: when green flag clicked is yellow (Events), go to x: y: and point in direction are blue (Motion), and the purple blocks are in Looks.

Drag the cat somewhere else on the stage with your mouse, then click the green flag. The cat should jump to the middle, face right, and say "Flag works!" for two seconds.

This script is also a reset: it puts the cat back the way it started. Almost every project in this course begins with a reset script like this one, because Scratch remembers where things were when the last run ended.

#Test 2: The keyboard

Add two more scripts beside the first. Use the dropdown on when space key pressed to pick the arrow keys.

Click once on the stage, then press the arrow keys. The cat should step 20 pixels per press, and the x box under the stage should count up and down by 20.

Clicking the stage first matters. Key presses go to whatever part of the screen you clicked last. If you last clicked the browser's address bar, your arrows move a text cursor instead of the cat.

#Test 3: The mouse

Click the cat. It changes color with each click. Click 8 times and it's orange again: the color effect wraps around every 200, and 8 × 25 = 200. Test 1 also clears the effect, so the green flag fixes the color too.

#Test 4: The speakers

Press the space bar. You should hear a meow, and only after it finishes does the cat ask its question. That's what "until done" means: the script waits for the sound to end before moving to the next block. You'll see in Module 4 why that waiting can freeze a game.

#Test 5: Save, close, and reopen

A project you can't reopen isn't really saved. Pick the tab that matches how you use Scratch:

No account

  1. Click File › Save to your computer. Your browser saves a file called Scratch Project.sb3, usually into Downloads (some browsers ask where to put it).
  2. Rename it systems-check.sb3 and move it into a folder named Scratch course.
  3. Click File › New. The editor resets to a fresh cat.
  4. Click File › Load from your computer, pick systems-check.sb3, and press the green flag.

With an account

  1. Click the title box in the menu bar and name the project Systems check.
  2. Click File › Save now. A short "Project saved." message appears.
  3. Click the folder icon (My Stuff) at the top of the Scratch website. Your project is in the list.
  4. Click its title, then See inside, and press the green flag.

Scratch app

  1. Click File › Save to your computer. A normal save window opens; name the file systems-check.sb3 and put it in a folder named Scratch course.
  2. Close the app completely, then open it again.
  3. Click File › Load from your computer, pick your file, and press the green flag.

If all five tests pass, this is what you saw:

#When a test fails

  • Arrows do nothing, but clicking works. Click the stage and try again. If you're using a laptop with an on-screen keyboard or a remote desktop, try a physical keyboard.
  • Silent space bar. Go back to the no-sound fix in the last lesson. Also check the Sounds tab: if the Meow sound was deleted, the block's dropdown will be empty.
  • Can't find the saved file. Look in Downloads, and search your computer for .sb3. Then change your browser's download setting so it asks where to save each file.
  • The project opens, but scripts are missing. You probably loaded an older copy. Check the file's date and keep just one copy in your course folder.

Keep systems-check.sb3. It's your known-good project: if it ever stops working, the problem is the computer, not your code.

Check your understanding

2 questions

1The arrow keys don't move the cat, but clicking the cat still changes its color. What should you try first?

  • Key presses go to the last thing you clicked. Clicking the stage sends them to Scratch.

  • Clicks are reaching the project, so Scratch itself is working; it's a focus problem.

  • A bigger step won't help if the key presses never reach the script.

Show answer

A. Key presses go to the last thing you clicked. Clicking the stage sends them to Scratch.

2You drag the cat to the top-left corner and press the green flag. Where does it end up?

  • The first block after the hat moves it, so it can't stay in the corner.

  • go to x: (0) y: (0) and point in direction (90) run first, so the reset puts it back.

  • Stopping doesn't move sprites, but the reset script does on the next flag click.

Show answer

B. go to x: (0) y: (0) and point in direction (90) run first, so the reset puts it back.

#Further reading

  • Project Editor on the Scratch Wiki (opens in a new tab): every part of the editor, with screenshots, written by Scratch users.
  • Scratch Ideas (opens in a new tab): the official tutorials and coding cards, handy when you want a second explanation.

m1-l3.html:
What you'll learn

  • Explain what the Notes, Build-along, and Practice lessons in each module are for.
  • Save versions of a project so a bad change never costs you more than a few minutes.
  • Move scripts and sprites between projects with the Backpack or with sprite files.
  • Use a five-step routine, and the editor's own tools, to find out why a script misbehaves.
  • Ask for help in a way that gets a useful answer.

Here's the most common way Scratch projects get lost, and it isn't a crash. Someone saves Scratch Project.sb3 into Downloads, then saves again the next day, and the browser names it Scratch Project (1).sb3, then (2), then (3). A week later there are six files with the same name and nobody remembers which one has the working jump. Ten minutes of routine now prevents all of that.

#How this course fits together

Module 1 is setup. Modules 2 to 7 each teach one big idea in three lessons:

Lesson What you do Time to plan for
Notes Learn the idea with small examples, then check yourself with a quiz 30 to 45 minutes
Build-along Build one real game or scene step by step 45 to 90 minutes
Practice Solve new problems with hints and full solutions, then try a challenge 45 to 90 minutes

Module 8 is your capstone: a multi-level game you design, build, test, and present. It uses something from every module, so don't skip ahead.

Two habits make the lessons work much better. First, keep Scratch open next to the lesson and build as you read. Second, when a lesson asks you to predict what a script will do, actually decide before you click. Being wrong about a prediction teaches you more than reading the answer.

#Save early, and keep old versions

Each way of running Scratch saves differently, but the rule is the same: save after every step that works.

No account

File › Save to your computer creates a new file each time. Use that to your advantage: give every save a version number.

If version 3 breaks badly, open version 2 and you've lost one step, not the whole game.

With an account

File › Save now saves to your account, and Scratch also saves on its own every so often. Before a risky change, like rewriting your movement script, use File › Save as a copy. You get a second project to experiment in while the original stays safe. Your copies all appear in My Stuff.

Scratch app

File › Save to your computer opens a save window. Use the same version numbers as in the No account tab, and keep every file in one course folder. On a Chromebook, export important projects to Google Drive now and then. Projects stored inside the app can be lost if the app is removed or the Chromebook is reset.

Two rescue tools are worth knowing before you need them:

  • Edit › Restore brings back the last sprite, costume, sound, or backdrop you deleted. It only remembers the most recent deletion, so use it right away.
  • Undo in the code area (right-click empty space and choose Undo, or press Ctrl+Z on Windows and Chromebook, Cmd+Z on Mac) takes back block moves and deletions.

#Organize your files and your project

Make one folder called Scratch course with a folder inside for each module. Name files module-project-version, like m4-reef-catch-v2.sb3. Future you will be grateful.

Inside a project, names matter even more, because your scripts use them:

  • Rename sprites in the sprite pane: Crab, not Sprite1. A block like touching (Sprite3 v)? tells you nothing, while touching (Jellyfish v)? reads like a sentence.
  • Name costumes for what they show: glow and dim, not costume1 and costume2.
  • Name variables for what they count: score, lives, fall speed.
  • Right-click the code area and choose Clean up Blocks to line your scripts up neatly. Add Comment sticks a note on the code area, or on a block if you right-click the block. Notes like "resets everything at the flag" help you later.

#Carry code between projects

Later modules reuse pieces of earlier games. There are two ways to move them.

With an account, use the Backpack. It's the bar along the bottom of the editor. Drag a script, sprite, costume, or sound onto it, open another project, and drag it back out. Your Backpack follows you to any computer you sign in on.

Without an account, export a sprite. Right-click the sprite in the sprite pane and choose export. You get a .sprite3 file with all of that sprite's scripts, costumes, and sounds. In another project, hover over the Choose a Sprite button and click Upload Sprite to bring it in.

#A routine for getting unstuck

Every programmer writes code that doesn't work. What separates beginners from experienced coders is mostly having a routine instead of staring at the screen. Here's one that fits Scratch:

  1. Say exactly what's wrong. "It's broken" can't be fixed. "The crab moves, but the score stays at 0 when it touches a starfish" can.
  2. Make it happen again on purpose. If you can't trigger the bug every time, you can't tell when you've fixed it.
  3. Run one script by itself. Click a script in the code area and it runs on its own, glowing yellow while it runs. If a script never glows, its hat block never fired.
  4. Look at the values. Tick the checkbox next to a variable, or next to x position, and a live monitor appears on the stage. Click any round reporter block to see its current value in a bubble. To watch a value inside a loop, drop in a temporary say block:
  1. Change one thing at a time, then test. If you change three things and it starts working, you don't know which one fixed it, or whether the other two broke something new.

Scratch has its own help for this. The Debug button in the menu bar opens a set of cards with strategies like Read Aloud, Slow It Down, Check the Values, and Take a Break, Step Away. Slowing down helps more often than you'd think: a temporary wait (1) seconds between blocks lets you watch each step happen.

💡 Tip

Read your script out loud as if you were the sprite, block by block, doing only what each block says. You'll often hear the bug: "go to the top... fall... touching the crab? No... fall... touching? No..." and realize the score block sits outside the loop.

#Asking for help so people can help you

If the routine doesn't crack it, ask. A good question has four parts:

  1. What you expected to happen.
  2. What happened instead.
  3. What you already tried.
  4. The script itself: a link to a shared project, or a screenshot of the code.

With an account, the Help with Scripts forum on the Scratch website is full of people who answer these. Never post your real name, school, or anything that says where you live, and remember that the Scratch Community Guidelines apply there too.

Check your understanding

2 questions

1You deleted a sprite by accident, then deleted a sound. Which can Edit › Restore bring back?

  • Restore only remembers the most recent deletion, which was the sound.

  • It undoes the last deletion only, so restore right after the mistake.

  • It doesn't keep a history of deletions, just the last one.

Show answer

B. It undoes the last deletion only, so restore right after the mistake.

2While your game runs, you watch the code area and the when I receive [start v] script never glows. What does that tell you?

  • A script glows while it runs. No glow means its hat block never fired.

  • The blocks inside never got a chance to run; the problem is before the script starts.

  • Scripts and messages work the same whether or not the project is saved.

Show answer

A. A script glows while it runs. No glow means its hat block never fired.

#Further reading

  • Debugging Scripts on the Scratch Wiki (opens in a new tab): more detective tricks, with examples of common bugs.
  • Backpack on the Scratch Wiki (opens in a new tab): exactly what the Backpack can hold and how it behaves.
  • Help with Scripts forum (opens in a new tab): where Scratchers help each other with code. Read a few threads before you post.

m2-l1.html:
What you'll learn

  • Read and write positions on the stage's x–y grid, from (−240, −180) to (240, 180).
  • Choose between go to, glide, change x by, and set x to for a move.
  • Point sprites with directions and pick a rotation style that keeps them upright.
  • Switch costumes, backdrops, and layers to change what the player sees.
  • Start scripts with event hat blocks, and predict what happens when several run at once.

Make a new project, drag out go to x: (300) y: (0), and click it. The cat doesn't go to 300. It stops at the right edge with part of its body still showing. Click go to x: (0) y: (-500) and the same thing happens at the bottom.

There's a reason: the stage is only 480 pixels wide and 360 tall, and Scratch won't let a sprite leave it completely. Every game you'll build depends on knowing exactly where things are on that small rectangle, so that's where we start.

#The stage is a 480 by 360 grid

Every point on the stage has two numbers. x says how far left or right, and y says how far up or down. The center is (0, 0).

  • x runs from −240 at the left edge to 240 at the right edge.
  • y runs from −180 at the bottom to 180 at the top.
  • Positive x is right of center, negative x is left. Positive y is above center, negative y is below.

Move your mouse over this practice stage to read coordinates the way Scratch does, and click to drop pins. (The code is only the web page that draws the grid; you don't need to read it.)

Try to land a pin on (−120, 60). It's left of center, so x is negative, and above center, so y is positive. If you can find a spot before you click, you can place sprites without guessing.

#A sprite's position is its costume center

When the sprite pane says a sprite is at x 100, y 50, it means one particular point of the sprite is there: its costume center. For the cat, that's roughly the middle of its body. When the sprite turns, it spins around that same point.

Four Motion blocks change position, and they behave differently:

Block What it does
go to x: () y: () Jumps straight to that point, with no animation
glide (1) secs to x: () y: () Travels there smoothly; the script waits until it arrives
change x by () Moves relative to where the sprite is now
set x to () Moves to an exact x and leaves y alone

Predict where the cat ends up, then build it and check the x and y boxes:

After this block x y
go to x: (-200) y: (-100) −200 −100
glide (2) secs… 0 −100
change x by (50) 50 −100
change y by (150) 50 50
set x to (-60) −60 50

Notice that change blocks add to whatever is there already, while set throws the old value away. Mixing them up is the most common source of "why is my sprite over there?"

#Direction: 90 means right

Scratch measures direction in degrees, like a compass that starts at the top:

Direction The sprite faces
0 up
90 right (every new sprite starts here)
180 down
−90 left

point in direction (-90) turns the cat to face left, but it also flips it upside down, because by default sprites rotate all around. For characters that walk left and right, pick a different rotation style:

Now the cat mirrors itself to face left and stays upright. The third style, don't rotate, keeps the costume exactly as drawn no matter the direction, which suits things like buttons and score signs.

#Costumes, backdrops, and layers

A costume is one picture of a sprite. Many library sprites come with two or more, and flipping between them quickly is how Scratch animation works. Open the Costumes tab to see them, rename them, or paint new ones.

next costume moves to the following costume in the list and wraps back to the first after the last. switch costume to picks one by name, which is safer when the order might change.

The Stage has its own pictures, called backdrops. Only the Stage owns backdrops, but any sprite can change them with switch backdrop to. Sprites are always drawn in front of the backdrop.

Sprites are also stacked in layers, like sheets of paper. When two sprites overlap, the one on the higher layer covers the other. go to [front v] layer moves a sprite to the top of the pile, and go [backward v] (1) layers sinks it one step. Dragging a sprite around the stage in the editor also brings it to the front.

#Events start scripts, and scripts run side by side

A script only runs when something starts it. That's the job of the round-topped hat blocks in Events:

Hat block Starts its script when…
when green flag clicked the green flag is clicked
when [space v] key pressed that key is pressed (the dropdown lists every key)
when this sprite clicked someone clicks this sprite
when backdrop switches to [ v] the Stage changes to that backdrop
when [loudness v] > (10) the microphone hears something loud, or the timer passes a number
when I receive [ v] another script sends that message with broadcast

A program built this way is called event-driven: nothing happens until an event arrives, and then every script waiting for that event starts. They don't take turns. They all run at the same time.

Here's one sprite with two scripts on the same hat block. Run it and both happen at once: the cat glides across the stage while it changes costume.

The last hat in the table, when I receive, is how sprites signal each other: one script broadcasts a message like start, and every script waiting for start begins. You'll use it once in the next lesson, and Module 3 is all about it.

⚠️ Watch out

Two scripts fighting over one sprite. If one script is gliding the cat and another does go to x: (0) y: (0), the jump seems to do nothing. The glide works out its position fresh every frame from where it started and where it's going, so on the very next frame it puts the cat back on its path. When a sprite won't go where you told it, look for another script that's also moving it.

⚠️ Watch out

No reset at the start. If your green flag script starts with a glide instead of a go to, every run begins wherever the last one ended. Start each sprite's green flag script by setting its position, direction, costume, and size.

Check your understanding

4 questions

1A sprite is at (100, 50). It runs change x by (-150) and then change y by (-100). Where is it now?

  • That's what two set blocks would do. change adds to the current position.

  • 100 − 150 = −50 for x, and 50 − 100 = −50 for y.

  • The changes are negative, so both numbers get smaller.

Show answer

B. 100 − 150 = −50 for x, and 50 − 100 = −50 for y.

2You want a car sprite to face down the stage. Which block?

  • 0 is up in Scratch, not down.

  • −90 is left.

  • 180 is straight down, the opposite of 0.

Show answer

C. 180 is straight down, the opposite of 0.

3A sprite has two green flag scripts. One says "Hello!" for 2 seconds; the other glides across the stage in 2 seconds. What do you see?

  • Scripts with the same hat don't take turns.

  • Both scripts start on the same click and run at the same time.

  • Where a script sits in the code area doesn't matter; every matching hat fires.

Show answer

B. Both scripts start on the same click and run at the same time.

4You run go to x: (0) y: (500). Where does the sprite end up?

  • Scratch doesn't let sprites leave the stage completely.

  • The stage only goes up to y = 180, and Scratch stops the sprite while a piece is still visible.

  • Scratch doesn't reset the sprite; it stops it at the edge.

Show answer

B. The stage only goes up to y = 180, and Scratch stops the sprite while a piece is still visible.

Key takeaways

  • The stage is 480 × 360: x from −240 to 240, y from −180 to 180, with (0, 0) in the center.
  • A sprite's x and y are the position of its costume center.
  • change moves relative to where you are; set and go to move to an exact spot; glide moves over time and makes the script wait.
  • Direction 90 is right, 0 is up, 180 is down, −90 is left. Use the left-right rotation style for walking characters.
  • Hat blocks start scripts, and every script triggered by the same event runs at the same time.

#Further reading

  • Coordinate System on the Scratch Wiki (opens in a new tab): the grid in more detail, with pictures of each quadrant.
  • Costume on the Scratch Wiki (opens in a new tab): how costumes, costume centers, and the costume list work.
  • Events Blocks on the Scratch Wiki (opens in a new tab): every hat block in the Events category, with examples.

m2-l2.html:
What you'll learn

  • Paint a sprite with two costumes and name them so scripts can use them.
  • Keep moving sprites inside a region of the stage by choosing coordinate ranges.
  • Run two scripts in one sprite at the same time, and stop them on purpose.
  • Use four different events: green flag, sprite click, key press, and a broadcast message.

It's night in the woods. Five fireflies drift between the trees, blinking on and off at their own pace. Click one and it zips into a glass jar in the corner and stays there, glowing. When you've caught enough, press the space bar: the woods brighten into morning and every firefly goes dark.

There's no score and no way to lose yet. This is a scene, not a game, but it uses every idea from the Notes: coordinates, costumes, layers, and scripts that start on events and run side by side.

#What we're building

Each sprite has a few short scripts, and each script waits for one event:

And here's where everything lives on the stage:

#Step 1: Make the woods dark

  1. Start a new project. Right-click the cat in the sprite pane and choose delete.
  2. Click Choose a Backdrop (bottom right) and pick Woods.
  3. Click the Stage panel on the far right so the code area shows the Stage's scripts, and build:

Click the green flag and the woods go dark. The brightness effect runs from −100 (black) to 100 (white), and −70 still leaves the trees faintly visible. Effects on the Stage only change the backdrop; sprites keep their own colors, which is exactly what lets a firefly glow against the dark.

#Step 2: Paint a firefly with two costumes

  1. Hover over Choose a Sprite and click the paintbrush (Paint).
  2. In the paint editor, pick the Circle tool. Set Fill to bright yellow and Outline to none (the crossed-out swatch).
  3. Hold Shift and drag a small circle, about the width of your fingertip on the screen, in the middle of the canvas. The middle of the canvas is the costume center, so drawing there keeps the firefly's x and y right on its body.
  4. In the Costume name box above the canvas, type glow.
  5. Right-click the costume thumbnail on the left and choose duplicate. Select the new costume, click the circle with the Select tool (the arrow), and change its fill to a dark olive green. Name this costume dim.
  6. In the sprite pane, rename the sprite Firefly.

#Step 3: Let it wander through the sky band

Select the Firefly and build its first script:

The pick random block is in Operators. Click the green flag and watch for a minute.

Every number here is a decision about the stage. x from −220 to 220 keeps the firefly a little away from the side edges. y from −40 to 160 keeps it above the ground and below the top edge. If you used glide (1) secs to (random position v) instead, the firefly would wander into the dirt and the jar. Picking the ranges yourself is how you keep a sprite in its part of the scene.

The glide time is random too, from 1 to 3 seconds. That small change makes the movement look alive instead of mechanical.

#Step 4: Blink with a second script

Add a second script to the same sprite:

Now the firefly wanders and blinks at the same time, because both scripts start on the green flag and run side by side. Notice the 0.5 in pick random: when either number has a decimal point, Scratch picks decimals like 1.37 instead of whole numbers. That's what makes each pause slightly different.

#Step 5: Catch it with a click

Here's a tempting first try. Build it and click the firefly:

The firefly starts toward the corner, then gets yanked back into the sky. The wander script is still running, and its glide wins on the very next frame. This is the "two scripts fighting over one sprite" bug from the Notes, live.

The fix is to stop the other scripts first. Replace the script with this one:

stop [other scripts in sprite v] (in Control; pick the option from the dropdown on stop all) halts the wander and blink scripts for this firefly only. Then it lights up, plays a sound, and glides into the jar. Add the Fairydust sound first: open the Sounds tab, click Choose a Sound, and search for it.

The landing spot is random within a small box, so caught fireflies don't all stack on the same pixel.

#Step 6: Put the jar in the corner

Click Choose a Sprite and add Jar. Give it this script:

go to [back v] layer puts the jar behind every other sprite, so caught fireflies glow in front of the glass instead of disappearing behind it. say [] with an empty box clears any speech bubble left from the last run.

#Step 7: Fill the woods with five fireflies

Right-click Firefly in the sprite pane and choose duplicate. Do it four times. Each copy, named Firefly2 to Firefly5, gets its own costumes and all three scripts. Click the green flag: five fireflies, each starting in a different random spot and blinking out of step with the others.

📝 Note

Duplicating is the last thing you do, on purpose. If you find a bug now, you have to fix it in five sprites. Module 6 shows a better way, where one sprite makes copies of itself and every copy shares one set of scripts.

#Step 8: Bring on the morning

Click the Stage and add a script that sends a message:

To create the morning message, open the dropdown on broadcast, choose New message, and type morning. The loop raises brightness from −70 to 0 in ten small steps, so the sunrise takes one second instead of snapping.

Now every firefly needs to hear it. Add this script to each of the five fireflies (drag it onto the other sprites in the sprite pane to copy it):

And to the Jar:

One space bar press, one message, seven sprites reacting at once. That's what broadcasting is for.

#The finished project

Sprite Scripts
Stage Green flag: Woods backdrop, brightness −70. Space key: broadcast morning, brighten in 10 steps.
Firefly (×5) Green flag: wander. Green flag: blink. Click: stop others, glow, sound, glide into the jar. morning: stop others, go dim.
Jar Green flag: corner, size 200%, back layer, clear bubble. morning: say good morning.

Test it like a player would:

  1. Click the green flag twice in a row. Everything resets both times: dark woods, an empty jar, no speech bubble.
  2. Catch one firefly, then click it again in the jar. It shuffles to a new spot inside the jar and stays there.
  3. Press space with two fireflies caught. All five go dark, the jar talks, and nothing keeps moving.
  4. Press space twice. The woods get brighter than normal the second time. (See the first idea below.)

Check your understanding

3 questions

1Why does the click script start with stop [other scripts in sprite v]?

  • It only affects the sprite it's in; the other fireflies keep wandering.

  • Without it, the wander glide overrides the glide to the jar every frame.

  • Sprites run many scripts at once; that's exactly why this one has to stop the others.

Show answer

B. Without it, the wander glide overrides the glide to the jar every frame.

2You change the wander script's y range to pick random (-180) to (180). What happens?

  • −180 is the bottom edge, so the band no longer stops above the ground.

  • Scratch only keeps sprites on the stage; where on the stage is up to your numbers.

  • Any number is allowed, so it runs and the fireflies just wander lower.

Show answer

A. −180 is the bottom edge, so the band no longer stops above the ground.

3Why put the jar on the back layer instead of the front?

  • Layers change what's drawn on top, not where a sprite is.

  • Sprites on higher layers cover lower ones, so the jar has to sit underneath.

  • Sprites are always in front of the backdrop, whatever their layer.

Show answer

B. Sprites on higher layers cover lower ones, so the jar has to sit underneath.

Key takeaways

  • Choose pick random ranges for x and y to keep a moving sprite in its own region of the stage.
  • Two scripts in one sprite run at the same time; stop [other scripts in sprite v] ends the ones you don't want.
  • Name costumes and switch by name, so your scripts still work if you reorder the costume list.
  • A broadcast lets one event, like a key press, start scripts in many sprites at once.

#Ideas to extend it

  • Morning only once. Pressing space twice over-brightens the woods. Start the space script with set [brightness v] effect to (-70) so the sunrise always starts from night.
  • Crickets. Add the Crickets sound to the Stage and play it with forever and play sound (Crickets v) until done in its own green flag script.
  • Shy fireflies. Make a firefly glide away if the mouse gets close. You'll need distance to (mouse-pointer v) from Sensing and an if block, which Module 3 covers.
  • Count the catch. Module 3 adds variables, so the jar can say how many fireflies you caught.

#Further reading

  • Paint Editor on the Scratch Wiki (opens in a new tab): every tool in the editor, vector and bitmap modes, and keyboard shortcuts.
  • Stop () on the Scratch Wiki (opens in a new tab): the difference between all, this script, and other scripts in sprite.
  • Glide () Secs to X: () Y: () on the Scratch Wiki (opens in a new tab): how glide works, including why the script waits for it.

m2-l3.html:
What you'll learn

  • Predict a sprite's position after a mix of go to, change, and set blocks.
  • Measure how Scratch's edge fence treats big and small sprites.
  • Choose directions and rotation styles for a walking character.
  • Control layers, stop runaway scripts, and react to backdrop changes.
  • Read one sprite's position from another sprite's script.

Each exercise starts from a new project unless it says otherwise. Try it on your own first, open the hint if you stall for more than a few minutes, and only then check the solution.

#Warm-up: where does it end?

Without building it, work out the final x and y:

Show solution

(−70, 60). Step by step: (30, −40), then x becomes 30 − 100 = −70, then y is set to 90 (the −40 is thrown away), then 90 − 30 = 60. Build it and check the sprite pane to confirm.

#Exercise 1: Say where you are

Make the cat say its own coordinates for two seconds whenever it's clicked. Drag it somewhere and click it:

Need a hint?

join in Operators glues two pieces of text together. You need to glue three pieces: the x position, a comma and space, and the y position. Put one join inside another.

Show solution

The inner join makes , 60, and the outer one puts the x in front. If you see long decimals after dragging, wrap each position in round from Operators: (round (x position)). Keep this script around; clicking a sprite to ask where it is beats squinting at the sprite pane.

#Exercise 2: How far past the edge can a sprite go?

Run this with the cat at its normal size, then again after set size to (20) %. Write down what it says each time.

Before running it, predict: will it say 400, 240, or something else?

Need a hint?

Look at how much of the cat is still showing at the right edge. Scratch keeps a small strip of every sprite on the stage, measured from the sprite's edge, not its center.

Show solution

It says neither 400 nor 240. The full-size cat stops at a number noticeably bigger than 240, and the small cat stops much closer to 240.

Scratch doesn't fence the costume center; it fences the picture. It lets the sprite slide off until only a thin strip, at most about 15 pixels, is left on the stage. A wide sprite's center is far from its edge, so its center can sit well past 240. A tiny sprite's center is close to its edge, so it stops nearly at 240.

This matters for games. A check like if <(x position) > (240)> might never be true for a small sprite, so use a limit a little inside the edge, like 230.

#Exercise 3: Face the way you walk

Make the cat walk with the arrow keys. Left and right should turn it to face that way and step 10. Up and down should move it 10 without turning it. It must never end up upside down.

Need a hint?

move (10) steps moves in whatever direction the sprite is facing. Which rotation style mirrors a sprite instead of spinning it?

Show solution

Left and right use point in direction plus move, so the cat turns and walks. Up and down use change y by because move would send the cat in the direction it's facing, which is sideways. The left-right rotation style mirrors the costume when the direction is negative instead of rotating it upside down.

#Exercise 4: Put everyone in the right layer

Add the Sun, Cloud, and Dove sprites, and drag them so they overlap. When the green flag is clicked, the order from back to front must always be: Sun, then Cloud, then Dove, no matter how you dragged them before. Then the Dove glides from (−200, 60) to (200, 60) over 4 seconds, passing in front of the cloud.

Need a hint?

You only need two layer blocks in total, in two different sprites. With three sprites, if you know which one is at the very back and which is at the very front, where does that leave the third?

Show solution

Sun:

Dove:

The Cloud needs no layer block. The Sun is forced to the back and the Dove to the front, so the Cloud has to be in the middle. This is more reliable than giving all three sprites layer blocks, because green flag scripts in different sprites start at the same moment and you can't count on which one runs first.

#Exercise 5: Stop the legs when the walk ends

Add the Avery Walking sprite and give it these two scripts:

Avery walks across nicely, then keeps marching on the spot after she arrives. Fix it so her legs stop when the glide ends and she shows her first costume.

Need a hint?

The glide script knows when the walk is over, because the block after glide only runs once the glide has finished. Which block can end the other script from there?

Show solution

glide makes its script wait, so the stop block runs exactly when she arrives. It ends the animation loop, and switch costume to puts her in a standing pose. Leave the forever script as it is; it still starts on every green flag.

#Exercise 6: Switch scenes with backdrop events

Give the Stage two backdrops, Arctic and Beach Malibu. Pressing 1 shows the Arctic and pressing 2 shows the beach. Add Penguin 2, which reacts to each scene on its own:

The scripts that press the keys must not mention the penguin at all.

Need a hint?

The Stage handles the keys with switch backdrop to. The penguin listens with a hat block from Events that fires when the backdrop changes.

Show solution

Stage:

Penguin 2:

The Stage changes the scene and the penguin decides for itself what that means. Add a third sprite that reacts to the same backdrops and you won't touch the Stage's scripts at all. Keeping the "what happened" separate from the "who cares" is the core idea of event-driven programs.

#Challenge: A mirror twin

Make a second cat that always stands at the mirror image of the first one across the vertical center line, as if the y-axis were a mirror. Steer the first cat with your arrow-key scripts from Exercise 3. When the first cat is at (120, 60), the twin is at (−120, 60). When the first cat faces right, the twin faces left.

Move over this practice stage to see the rule: the orange dot follows your mouse, and the blue dot is its twin.

Need a hint?

In Sensing, ([x position v] of (Sprite1 v)) reads another sprite's x. The twin's x is that number with its sign flipped, which you can get by subtracting it from 0. Directions mirror the same way: 90 becomes −90.

Show solution

Duplicate the cat, delete the copy's arrow-key scripts, and give the twin (Sprite2) this script:

Every frame, the twin copies the first cat's y and the opposite of its x and direction. There's no -x block in Scratch, so 0 − x does the flipping. For an extra twist, add a third cat that mirrors across the horizontal line instead: same x, opposite y.

m3-l1.html:
What you'll learn

  • Replace matched wait timers with broadcast so several sprites start at exactly the right moment.
  • Choose between broadcast and broadcast and wait.
  • Make variables for all sprites or for one sprite, and reset them at the start.
  • Write conditions with comparisons, and, or, and not, and use wait until and repeat until.
  • Track what mode a game is in with a state variable.

Here's a race start that seems to work. The referee counts down, and the runner waits the same amount of time before taking off:

The first script is the referee; the second belongs to the runner. Now make "Ready..." last 2 seconds for drama. The runner leaves on "Set...", because its wait (2) has no idea the referee changed. Add four more runners and you have five separate timers to keep in sync by hand. Scripts timed this way break the moment anything about the timing changes.

#Broadcasts: one sender, many listeners

The fix is to have the referee tell everyone when to go. broadcast sends a message; every script that starts with when I receive for that message begins at once, in every sprite and on the Stage.

Now the runners don't keep time at all. Change the countdown however you like and they still leave on "GO!".

Three rules cover almost everything about broadcasts:

  1. Every matching when I receive script starts, however many there are.
  2. The sender keeps going right away. The blocks after broadcast don't wait for anyone.
  3. If nobody is listening, nothing happens and there's no error message. A broadcast to an empty room is silent.

#broadcast and wait: when order matters

Sometimes the sender needs to wait. Say a title card should explain the controls before the game starts. With broadcast and wait, the sender pauses until every script that received the message has finished:

The first script is on the Stage; the second belongs to an Instructions sprite. The Stage waits the full three seconds, then sends start game. If you make the instructions longer later, the game still starts at the right time.

⚠️ Watch out

A broadcast and wait that never returns. If any receiving script contains a forever loop, it never finishes, so the sender waits forever and the game freezes before it starts. Use broadcast and wait only for messages whose receivers end on their own.

#Variables: the game's memory

A variable is a named box that holds one value, like a score, a number of lives, or a word. Click Make a Variable in the Variables category, type a name, and choose:

  • For all sprites: one shared box that every sprite and the Stage can read and change. Use it for things the whole game cares about, like score.
  • For this sprite only: each sprite gets its own private box. Use it for things like each enemy's health. Other sprites can only read it, using the of block in Sensing.

Variables made on the Stage are always for all sprites.

set replaces the value; change adds to it (use a negative number to subtract). Tick the checkbox beside a variable to show its monitor on the stage. Right-click the monitor to switch between a normal readout, a large readout, and a slider.

Two facts trip people up. First, a variable keeps its value after you press the stop sign, and even after you save and reopen the project, so every game needs a set at the start. Second, a variable can hold words as well as numbers: set [state v] to [playing] is perfectly fine, and it's the basis of game states below.

#Conditions, and loops that wait for them

A condition is a pointy block that's either true or false. The green Operators blocks build them:

Block True when…
<(score) > (9)> score is more than 9
<(lives) = (0)> lives is exactly 0
<<(score) > (9)> and <(lives) > (0)>> both are true
<<key (a v) pressed?> or <key (l v) pressed?>> at least one is true
<not <(state) = [playing]>> state is anything except playing

Text comparisons ignore capital letters in Scratch, so <[Playing] = [playing]> is true.

Conditions go in if blocks, which run their inside once if the condition is true, and in two loops that wait for a condition. wait until pauses a script until something becomes true. repeat until repeats its inside until something becomes true:

Both loops check their condition again every frame, about 30 times a second. Neither needs a forever around it, and that's a good thing, as you'll see in the next warning.

⚠️ Watch out

A broadcast inside forever restarts its receiver every frame. When a message arrives for a script that's already running, Scratch restarts that script from the top. So this never works:

Once the score passes 9, level up is sent 30 times a second. The receiver keeps restarting its 2-second say, so the bubble never goes away and level never changes. Send the message once instead: replace the forever and if with wait until <(score) > (9)>, then broadcast (level up v).

#Game states: what mode is the game in?

Most games have modes: a title screen, a countdown, play, pause, game over. The same key might do different things in each, or nothing at all. Keep the current mode in a variable called state, and change it at each turning point:

Then every input checks the state before acting:

In the title screen, pressing space does nothing here, because the state isn't playing yet. Broadcasts and states work as a pair: a broadcast says "something just happened," and the state variable remembers "this is the mode we're in now."

⚠️ Watch out

The score starts at 14. If the green flag script doesn't set [score v] to (0), the score carries over from the last game. The same goes for lives, state, and every other variable. Reset them all in one place, usually a green flag script on the Stage.

Check your understanding

4 questions

1The referee runs broadcast (go v) and then say [sent]. The runner runs when I receive [go v], wait (1) seconds, say [got it]. Which bubble appears first?

  • broadcast doesn't wait, so the referee says "sent" right away while the runner is still waiting its 1 second.

  • The runner has to wait 1 second first, and the referee isn't held up by the broadcast.

  • They'd only be close if the runner had no wait.

Show answer

A. broadcast doesn't wait, so the referee says "sent" right away while the runner is still waiting its 1 second.

2Same scripts, but the referee uses broadcast (go v) and wait. Now what?

  • broadcast and wait holds the referee until the runner's script ends.

  • The referee waits for the runner's whole script, including the 1-second wait and the say, before moving on.

  • It would only freeze if the runner's script never ended.

Show answer

B. The referee waits for the runner's whole script, including the 1-second wait and the say, before moving on.

3Once the score passes 9, a "Level up!" bubble appears and never goes away, and level stays at 1. What's the likely cause?

  • That would stop other sprites from changing it, but it wouldn't keep the bubble on screen.

  • The receiver restarts every frame, so its 2-second say never finishes and the change never runs.

  • Any block works in a receiver; the problem is the receiver restarting.

Show answer

B. The receiver restarts every frame, so its 2-second say never finishes and the change never runs.

4Three Ghost sprites each have a health variable made "for this sprite only." You click Ghost2 and its script runs change [health v] by (-1). Whose health changes?

  • That's what would happen with one variable for all sprites.

  • Each sprite has its own private copy, and the script changes the copy belonging to its own sprite.

  • The sprite that owns a local variable can change it freely.

Show answer

B. Each sprite has its own private copy, and the script changes the copy belonging to its own sprite.

Key takeaways

  • Use broadcast instead of matching wait timers, so sprites react to events instead of guessing when they'll happen.
  • broadcast and wait holds the sender until every receiving script finishes; never use it with a receiver that loops forever.
  • Variables keep their values between runs, so reset every one at the green flag.
  • wait until and repeat until check a condition every frame; you rarely need forever plus if around a broadcast.
  • A state variable records the game's current mode, and every input should check it before acting.

#Further reading

  • Broadcast on the Scratch Wiki (opens in a new tab): how messages work, with examples and the restart rule.
  • Broadcast () and Wait on the Scratch Wiki (opens in a new tab): when the sender resumes, with common uses.
  • Variable on the Scratch Wiki (opens in a new tab): global and local variables, monitors, and cloud variables.

m3-l2.html:
What you'll learn

  • Use broadcast and wait so a countdown can't begin until every racer is in place.
  • Track the game's mode in a state variable and check it before every action.
  • Count a key press rather than a key being held, using wait until.
  • Guarantee exactly one winner per round, even in a photo finish.
  • Keep a first-to-three score across rounds.

Two players share one keyboard. Player 1 is a hare and mashes A; Player 2 is a dog and mashes L. A referee says "Ready... Set..." and blows a whistle, and both racers sprint across the field, one hop per key press. First to the finish line wins the round, and the first player to win three rounds wins the match.

Getting the fairness right is the real project. Nobody may move before the whistle. Holding a key down must not count as mashing it. If both racers hit the line in the same instant, only one of them can be crowned. Each of those rules is a few blocks of variables, conditions, and broadcasts.

#What we're building

The whole game moves through five states. The state variable always holds the current one, and broadcasts announce each change:

#Step 1: Set up the track

  1. Start a new project and delete the cat. Choose the Playing Field backdrop.
  2. Add three library sprites: Referee, Hare, and Dog2.
  3. Add the Line sprite and rename it Finish.
  4. In Variables, make four variables, all For all sprites: state, winner, wins 1, and wins 2. Untick state and winner so their monitors hide; keep wins 1 and wins 2 showing. Right-click each wins monitor and pick large readout.

The Line sprite is a long horizontal stroke. Turned to direction 0, it stands up and becomes a finish line across both lanes:

That's the Finish sprite's only script.

#Step 2: Take your places

The referee resets the match and starts the first round. Give the Referee these two scripts:

Each racer answers places by walking back to its lane. Hare:

Dog2 gets the same script with dog2-a and y: (-90).

Click the green flag. Both racers glide to the start line, and only then does the referee say "Press space". That ordering is the whole point of broadcast and wait: the referee is held until both places scripts finish. With a plain broadcast, it would set the state to waiting immediately, and an eager player could start a countdown while the racers were still walking back.

#Step 3: A countdown nobody can time

Add this script to the Referee. Make the go message from the broadcast dropdown as before.

Three decisions are hiding in here:

  • The if means space only works while the game is waiting. Pressing it mid-race does nothing.
  • "Set..." lasts a random time between 1 and 2.5 seconds. If it were always the same, players would learn the rhythm and press on the beat instead of reacting to the whistle.
  • state becomes racing before the go broadcast, so anything that starts on go can already trust the state.

#Step 4: Run, but only when the key is tapped

Here's the obvious way to make the hare run. Try it on the Hare:

Start a race and hold A instead of tapping it. After a short pause the hare zooms off by itself. Your keyboard repeats a held key, the same way holding a letter in a text box types it over and over, and each repeat fires the hat block again. Holding beats mashing, so that version is a cheat.

Delete that script. This one counts a press only after the key has been let go:

Read the loop as a story: wait for A to go down, hop 12 steps and switch legs, wait for A to come back up, and repeat until the finish line. Holding A now gives exactly one hop. From x = −200 to the line takes about 30 taps.

Give Dog2 the same script with the l key.

#Step 5: Exactly one winner

When the loop ends, the racer has touched the finish. Add these blocks to the bottom of the Hare's go script, after the repeat until loop:

Why check the state? Picture a photo finish: both racers touch the line in the same frame. Scratch still runs the two scripts one after the other. The first one sees racing, claims the win, and changes the state to finished. The second sees finished and skips the if. Without that check, both players would score.

Both racers also need to react to the result. Add this to the Hare:

stop [other scripts in sprite v] ends the loser's running loop, which would otherwise keep waiting for key presses. Dog2's versions use Player 2 and wins 2.

#Step 6: Punish false starts

Mashing during "Ready... Set..." should cost you. Add this to the Hare (and with l to Dog2):

The same key now means three different things depending on the state: a penalty during countdown, nothing at all here during racing (the go script handles running), and nothing while waiting.

#Step 7: First to three

The referee announces each result and decides whether to start another round:

new round sends everyone back through places, so the next round always starts from a clean line.

#The finished game

Sprite Scripts
Referee Green flag: reset wins, go to corner, broadcast new round. new round: placing, places and wait, waiting. Space: countdown with random "Set", racing, go, whistle. finish: announce, then match over or new round.
Hare places: walk to (−200, 40). go: tap loop with A, then claim the win if still racing. finish: stop others, cheer or sulk. A key: false-start penalty during countdown.
Dog2 Same as the Hare with the L key, y = −90, Player 2, and wins 2.
Finish Green flag: stand up at x = 200.

Playtest with a friend, and also try to break it:

  1. Hold A for the whole race. The hare hops once.
  2. Tap A during "Set...". The hare jumps back 40 and says "False start!".
  3. Press space during a race. Nothing happens.
  4. Win three rounds. The referee announces the match and stops starting new rounds.

Check your understanding

3 questions

1The referee uses broadcast (places v) and wait before setting the state to waiting. What goes wrong if it uses plain broadcast (places v)?

  • A plain broadcast still starts their places scripts.

  • Without the wait, the referee doesn't hold for the glides to finish before accepting the start.

  • Both blocks are valid; the bug is about timing, not an error message.

Show answer

B. Without the wait, the referee doesn't hold for the glides to finish before accepting the start.

2Why does "Set..." last a random time?

  • It actually makes the countdown longer on average.

  • Any number works there.

  • A fixed countdown can be timed; a random one can't.

Show answer

C. A fixed countdown can be timed; a random one can't.

3Both racers touch the finish line in the same frame. Who scores?

  • That's what would happen without the if <(state) = [racing]> check.

  • It changes the state to finished, so the second script's if fails.

  • One script always runs first and claims the win.

Show answer

B. It changes the state to finished, so the second script's if fails.

Key takeaways

  • broadcast and wait is how you say "don't continue until everyone is ready."
  • A state variable lets one key mean different things in different modes, and lets you ignore input when it shouldn't count.
  • wait until key pressed, then wait until not pressed, counts taps and ignores held keys.
  • Checking and changing the state in the same script prevents two winners in a tie.
  • Reset match-long variables on the green flag and round-long ones at the start of each round.

  • Reaction time. Add reset timer right after the whistle, and when a racer makes its first hop, say the timer value. Who reacts faster?
  • A computer opponent. Replace Dog2's key loop with repeat until <touching (Finish v)?>, change x by (12), wait (pick random (0.12) to (0.2)) seconds. Tune the wait for easy, medium, and hard.
  • Four players. Add two more racers with their own keys and lanes. What has to change in the referee's scripts?
  • A crowd. Play Cheer when someone wins the match.

m4-l1.html:
What you'll learn

  • Convert between steps per frame and steps per second, and explain what happens on each pass of a game loop.
  • Make a sprite ease toward a target, and tune how snappy or floaty it feels.
  • Animate a sprite at a sensible speed, only while it's moving.
  • Use start sound and play sound until done in the right places.
  • Use graphic effects and size changes as feedback, and reset them properly.
  • Write scoring and edge rules that are fair and that players can see.

Picture two catch games with exactly the same rules. In the first, the catcher snaps to the mouse, the falling object just vanishes when caught, and the score ticks up in silence. In the second, the catcher swings smoothly after the mouse, its claws snap as it moves, a catch makes it bounce with a rising chime and a sparkle, and getting stung flashes it white. Players will tell you the second one is more fun, but it doesn't have a single extra rule. It has maybe fifteen extra blocks of feedback.

Game designers call that feedback juice. This lesson covers the pieces: frames, easing, animation, sound, and effects. Then it covers the part juice can't fix, which is rules that feel unfair.

#Scratch thinks in frames

Scratch redraws the stage about 30 times a second. Each redraw is a frame. When a loop moves or changes a sprite, Scratch runs one pass of that loop, redraws, and then runs the next pass. So the numbers in a game loop are per frame:

4 steps per frame × 30 frames per second = 120 steps per second. Crossing the 480-step-wide stage takes about 4 seconds. When a speed feels wrong, do this arithmetic first.

Almost every game repeats the same four jobs on every pass of its main loop:

For time that has to be measured in real seconds, like a countdown, use wait blocks or the timer in Sensing, not a count of frames. A slow computer can drop frames, but the timer keeps counting real seconds.

#Easing: move part of the way, every frame

There are three ways to make a sprite follow the mouse, and they feel completely different.

  • go to (mouse-pointer v) in a forever loop jumps there instantly. It feels stiff, like a cursor, not a character.
  • glide (0.5) secs to (mouse-pointer v) heads for where the mouse was, and its script can't do anything else until the glide ends. It feels laggy.
  • Easing moves a fraction of the remaining distance every frame:

(mouse x) - (x position) is the gap between where the sprite is and where it wants to be. Dividing by 5 moves it one fifth of that gap each frame. When the gap is 200, it moves 40. Next frame the gap is 160, so it moves 32. As it gets close, the steps shrink, so the sprite glides fast and then settles gently.

The divisor is a feel knob. Divide by 2 and the sprite is snappy, covering half the gap each frame. Divide by 15 and it floats, like something underwater. Easing works on anything with a target: a camera, a health bar sliding to its new value, a menu sliding in.

#Animation at the right speed

Switching costumes is animation, and speed is everything. Flip a costume every frame (30 times a second) and legs blur; flip once a second and it looks like a slideshow. About 6 to 12 changes a second looks like walking or flapping.

Put the animation in its own script, with its own wait, so it never slows down the movement loop. And animate only when there's something to animate:

Here speed is a variable the movement script sets each frame, and abs (in the of block in Operators) drops the minus sign, so moving left counts too. Standing still, the costume holds. Moving, it changes about 8 times a second.

#Sound: start it, don't wait for it

Two Sound blocks look almost the same and behave very differently:

  • start sound (pop v) starts the sound and moves on immediately.
  • play sound (pop v) until done starts the sound and waits for it to finish.

Inside a game loop, waiting is a disaster. A 0.6-second sound with until done freezes that loop for 0.6 seconds, about 18 frames with no movement and no collision checks. Use start sound for effects.

play sound until done is right for music, in a script of its own:

Here waiting is the point: the loop starts the music again only when it ends. Sound effects can also carry information. change [pitch v] effect by (20) raises every later sound from that sprite, so a chime that climbs with each catch tells the player their streak is growing without a single word. clear sound effects puts the pitch back.

#Graphic effects are feedback

Looks blocks can change how a sprite is drawn without changing its costume:

Effect Range Good for
ghost 0 (solid) to 100 (invisible) fading in and out
brightness −100 (black) to 100 (white) a hit flash, a night scene
color wraps around every 200 power-ups, rainbow cycles
fisheye, whirl, pixelate, mosaic 0 and up dizziness, teleports, glitches
size (set size to () %) any percent a squash or pop when something happens

Three patterns cover most needs:

The first is a flash, the second a pop, and the third a fade-out. Effects stay until something resets them, so start every sprite's game with clear graphic effects. Otherwise a sprite that faded out at the end of the last game starts the next one invisible.

⚠️ Watch out

A ghosted sprite still collides. A sprite with the ghost effect at 100 is invisible, but touching still sees it. If an enemy fades out and keeps hurting the player, that's why. Use hide to take a sprite out of play; hidden sprites never count as touching.

#Fair rules: scores, misses, and edges

Juice can't save a game whose rules feel like cheating. A few rules of thumb:

  1. Only spawn what can be caught or dodged. If the catcher can reach x from −200 to 200, drop things in that range, not at x = 235.
  2. Count once. When something is caught, change the score and move or hide the object in the same pass of the loop, so it can't be counted again on the next frame.
  3. Decide what each edge means. For a falling object, the bottom edge is a miss. For something drifting sideways, the side edges might wrap it around to the other side. For a ball, they bounce it. Pick the rule on purpose for each sprite.
  4. Show every rule. If missing costs a life, play a sound and flash something. Players accept a hard rule they can see; they hate one they can't.

For a wrap, check a little inside the edge:

Scratch won't let a sprite go fully off the stage, and for a small sprite it stops it with its center very close to 240. A check of > (240) might never be true. Using 230 means the wrap always fires.

Check your understanding

4 questions

1A loop runs change x by (6) and redraws every pass. About how far does the sprite move in 2 seconds?

  • That's 6 × 2, as if the loop ran once a second.

  • 6 steps per frame × 30 frames a second × 2 seconds = 360.

  • That's 6 × 10; Scratch runs about 30 frames a second, not 10.

Show answer

B. 6 steps per frame × 30 frames a second × 2 seconds = 360.

2A sprite at x = 0 eases toward x = 100 with change x by (((100) - (x position)) / (4)). Where is it after one frame?

  • Easing moves only part of the way each frame.

  • The gap is 100, and 100 ÷ 4 = 25.

  • The 4 divides the gap; it isn't a step size.

Show answer

B. The gap is 100, and 100 ÷ 4 = 25.

3Every time the player grabs a coin, the whole game stutters for half a second. Which block is the likely cause?

  • The loop waits for the sound to finish, so nothing moves until it does.

  • That one doesn't wait, so the loop keeps going.

  • Changing a variable takes no noticeable time.

Show answer

A. The loop waits for the sound to finish, so nothing moves until it does.

4An enemy fades out with the ghost effect at 100, but the player still loses lives when walking through the empty spot. What's the fix?

  • The ghost effect tops out at 100, and it never affects collisions anyway.

  • Hidden sprites never count as touching, but ghosted ones do.

  • That would make the enemy visible again without fixing the collision.

Show answer

B. Hidden sprites never count as touching, but ghosted ones do.

Key takeaways

  • Game loop numbers are per frame, and Scratch runs about 30 frames a second.
  • Easing (change x by ((target − x) / n)) moves part of the remaining gap each frame; a bigger n feels floatier.
  • Run animations in their own script with a wait, and only animate while the sprite is moving.
  • Use start sound for effects and play sound until done only for music in its own loop.
  • Effects last until reset, so use clear graphic effects at the start, and hide (not ghost) to take a sprite out of play.
  • Fair rules: spawn within reach, count once, choose each edge's meaning, and make every rule visible.

#Further reading

  • Game Loop on the Scratch Wiki (opens in a new tab): how Scratch games organize their main loop.
  • Graphic Effects on the Scratch Wiki (opens in a new tab): every effect with pictures and its exact range.
  • Sound Blocks on the Scratch Wiki (opens in a new tab): each sound block, including pitch and pan effects.
