What you'll learn

  • Move a player with easing toward the mouse, and tune the feel with one number.
  • Animate the player only while it's moving, in a separate script.
  • Write catch, miss, and sting rules that are fair and that the player can see.
  • Add feedback: a squash, a pitch that climbs with a streak, a sparkle, and a hit flash.
  • Raise the difficulty a little with every catch, and end the game cleanly.

A crab scuttles along the sea floor, following your mouse. Starfish sink from the surface, slowly spinning; catch one and the crab bounces, a chime plays, and a sparkle bursts above it. Catch several in a row and each chime is higher than the last. Every so often a jellyfish drifts down, aimed at wherever the crab is right now. Three stings and the game is over.

You'll build the rules first, then layer feedback on top. Play it after each step and notice how much the feel changes even when the rules don't.

#Step 1: Set up the reef

  1. Start a new project and delete the cat. Choose the Underwater 1 backdrop.
  2. Add four library sprites: Crab, Starfish, Jellyfish, and Star.
  3. Make four variables For all sprites: score, lives, streak, and sink speed. Then select the Crab and make one variable For this sprite only: speed.
  4. Keep the score, lives, and streak monitors on the stage, and untick the other two.

The Stage runs the game. It resets every variable, tells the sprites to start, and watches for the end:

Why do the sprites wait for start instead of using their own green flag scripts? Because then they're guaranteed to start after the reset. If the starfish and the Stage both began on the green flag, the starfish might read sink speed before the Stage had set it.

#Step 2: A crab that eases after the mouse

Select the Crab:

Each frame, the crab covers one sixth of the gap between itself and the mouse. Move the mouse quickly and the crab hurries; as it gets close, it slows and settles. Storing the step in speed before using it means another script can read how fast the crab is going, which you'll need in a moment.

🧪 Try it yourself

Change the 6 to 2, then to 15, and play for ten seconds each. At 2 the crab is twitchy and easy to steer; at 15 it's graceful but late. Pick the number that feels best to you. There's no right answer, only a feel you choose.

#Step 3: Claws that snap only while moving

The Crab has two costumes, crab-a and crab-b. Add a second script to the Crab:

When the crab is nearly still, speed is close to 0 and the claws hold. When it moves, they snap about eight times a second. Because this script has its own wait, it can't slow the movement loop down.

#Step 4: Starfish that sink, spin, and score

Select the Starfish:

Here are the game's rules, all in one loop:

  • Catch: +1 score, +1 streak, the next starfish sinks a little faster, and a caught message goes out. The starfish jumps back to the surface in the same pass, so it can't be counted twice.
  • Miss: reaching y = −170 costs nothing but your streak. That's a gentle rule on purpose: missing should sting a bit, not end the game.
  • Fair spawns: x from −210 to 210 means every starfish starts fully on screen, somewhere the crab can reach.

The turn right (3) degrees is pure decoration. A slowly spinning starfish looks like it's drifting through water instead of falling down a chute.

The two respawn lines are identical. Module 6 shows how to turn repeated blocks like these into one block of your own.

#Step 5: Make catching feel good

The rules work. Now three pieces of feedback, each reacting to caught.

A squash and a climbing chime. On the Crab, open the Sounds tab and add Collect from the library. Then:

The first catch in a streak plays a little above normal; each one after that plays higher. Players notice the climbing pitch long before they notice the streak counter.

A sparkle. The Star sprite bursts above the crab and fades:

Why not fade the starfish itself? Because a fading starfish is still in play, still touching the crab, and still scoring. A separate sprite that only looks like part of the catch can take as long as it likes.

#Step 6: Jellyfish that aim at you

Select the Jellyfish. It has four costumes that make it pulse:

Each jellyfish appears directly above where the crab is at that moment, then sinks one and a half times as fast as the starfish. Standing still gets you stung; moving makes it miss. It starts at the very top, so you always get a couple of seconds to react, and that's what keeps it fair.

Make the hit obvious. Add the Bonk sound to the Crab, then:

#Step 7: Music and the ending

Add Chill (or any loop you like) to the Stage's sounds, plus Lose:

The music loop uses play sound until done correctly: it's alone in its own script, so waiting hurts nothing. At game over, stop all sounds cuts the music, and the loop sees lives is 0 and ends.

Every sprite needs to stop at game over. Starfish, Jellyfish, and Star each get:

And the Crab stays on screen to announce the score:

#Step 8: Tune it

Play five games. If it's too easy or too hard, change one number at a time:

Knob Where Try
Crab responsiveness divisor in the crab's loop 4 to 10
Starting sink speed set [sink speed v] to (2) on the Stage 1.5 to 3
Difficulty ramp change [sink speed v] by (0.1) on the Starfish 0.05 to 0.2
Jellyfish frequency wait (pick random (1) to (3)) (2) to (5) for easier
Jellyfish speed (-1.5) * (sink speed) −1.2 to −2

#The finished game

Sprite Scripts
Stage Green flag: reset, start, wait for 0 lives, game over. start: music loop. game over: stop sounds, Lose.
Crab start: easing loop. start: claw animation. caught: pitch, chime, squash. stung: bonk, flash. game over: stop, show score.
Starfish start: sink, spin, catch and miss rules. game over: hide, stop.
Jellyfish start: aim, sink, sting rule. start: pulse. game over: hide, stop.
Star Green flag: hide. caught: sparkle. game over: hide, stop.

Check your understanding

3 questions

1Why is the sparkle a separate Star sprite instead of the starfish fading out?

  • Any sprite can use any graphic effect.

  • Ghosted sprites still collide, so the catch has to move the starfish away at once.

  • The sound comes from the Crab, not the Star.

Show answer

B. Ghosted sprites still collide, so the catch has to move the starfish away at once.

2The jellyfish goes to ([x position v] of (Crab v)) before it sinks. What does that do to the game?

  • It drops right where the crab is, so a crab that doesn't move gets stung.

  • It starts at the top, so there's time to move out of the way.

  • The x is set once, before the fall; the jellyfish doesn't steer.

Show answer

A. It drops right where the crab is, so a crab that doesn't move gets stung.

3Why do the crab, starfish, and jellyfish start on the start message instead of the green flag?

  • Both start scripts in the same frame.

  • The Stage broadcasts start only after its set blocks, so no sprite can read an old value.

  • Every sprite can have green flag scripts.

Show answer

B. The Stage broadcasts start only after its set blocks, so no sprite can read an old value.

Key takeaways

  • Easing toward the mouse feels alive, and its divisor is the one knob that sets the feel.
  • Animate in a separate script that reads the movement speed, so animation never slows the game.
  • Keep all the scoring rules in one loop, and move a caught object away in the same pass.
  • Feedback (squash, pitch, sparkle, flash) makes the same rules feel much better; give it its own sprites and scripts.
  • A Stage script that resets, broadcasts start, and waits for the end makes the start and finish of a game reliable.

#Ideas to extend it

  • A golden starfish. Give the Starfish a rare costume worth 5 points, using pick random and costume [name v] as in Module 3's practice.
  • Streak bonus. Every 5th catch in a streak, add 5 bonus points and make the sparkle bigger.
  • Hearts for lives. Replace the lives monitor with a Heart sprite that switches costumes for 3, 2, and 1 lives.
  • More starfish at once. Duplicating the Starfish sprite works, but Module 6 shows how clones make a whole shower of them from one sprite.

  • Stop () on the Scratch Wiki (opens in a new tab): what stop [other scripts in sprite v] does and doesn't end.
  • Timer on the Scratch Wiki (opens in a new tab): useful if you add a time limit or a survival clock to Reef Catch.

What you'll learn

  • Convert speeds between steps per frame and seconds.
  • Wrap a sprite around the stage edges reliably.
  • Time an animation with a frame counter and mod.
  • Chain easing so sprites follow each other.
  • Use the timer to make a short safe period after a hit.
  • Keep feedback (sounds, squashes, blinks) from blocking the game loop.

These exercises all use ideas from this module's Notes and from Reef Catch, but none of them repeats the build. Start each one in a new project.

#Warm-up: how long to cross?

A sprite starts at x = −200 and a forever loop runs change x by (5). About how many seconds until it reaches x = 200?

Show solution

About 2.7 seconds. The distance is 200 − (−200) = 400 steps. At 5 steps per frame that's 400 ÷ 5 = 80 frames, and at 30 frames per second, 80 ÷ 30 ≈ 2.7 seconds.

#Exercise 1: Fish that wrap around

Add two Fish sprites. The first swims right at 3 steps per frame; the second swims left at 2, facing left and right side up. When either reaches its edge, it reappears on the opposite side at the same height and keeps going.

Need a hint?

Check against 230 and −230, not 240 and −240. Scratch's edge fence can stop a sprite before its center ever passes 240. The left-swimming fish needs the left-right rotation style before you point it at −90.

Show solution

Fish:

Fish2:

Only x changes on a wrap, so each fish keeps its height. Pac-Man's side tunnel and the asteroids in Asteroids work the same way.

#Exercise 2: A walk cycle at the right speed

Add Pico Walking (costumes Pico walk1 to Pico walk4). In one forever loop, the arrow keys walk Pico left or right 4 steps per frame, facing the way it walks. While walking, the costume changes every 4th frame. While standing still, Pico shows Pico walk1. Use a frame variable, not a wait, for the timing.

Need a hint?

Add 1 to frame at the top of every pass. ((frame) mod (4)) = (0) is true on frames 4, 8, 12, and so on: once every 4 frames, or 7.5 times a second.

Show solution

A frame counter keeps the animation locked to the movement: if the computer slows down, the legs and the feet slow down together. Try mod (2) and mod (8) to see why 4 looks right at this walking speed.

#Exercise 3: A line of chicks

Add the Chick sprite and duplicate it twice. Chick follows the mouse with easing (gap ÷ 5, in both x and y). Chick2 eases toward Chick the same way, and Chick3 eases toward Chick2. Move the mouse in circles: the chicks should trail behind in a wobbly line.

Need a hint?

Chick2 doesn't need the mouse at all. Its target is ([x position v] of (Chick v)) and ([y position v] of (Chick v)).

Show solution

Chick:

Chick2 (Chick3 is the same with Chick2 in both of blocks):

Each chick lags behind the one ahead of it, so the lag adds up down the line, which is what makes the trail. When the mouse stops, they all settle into one spot. Push them apart with a bigger divisor for each chick, like 5, 7, and 9.

#Exercise 4: Two seconds of safety

Make a player sprite that eases after the mouse and a Shark 2 that glides back and forth across the middle of the stage. Touching the shark costs 1 of 3 lives. After a hit, the player blinks and can't be hurt again for 2 seconds. Without this, one pass through the shark costs every life at once.

Need a hint?

Keep a variable safe until. After a hit, set it to (timer) + (2). A touch only counts if timer is past safe until. Run the blink in a separate script triggered by a broadcast, so it never pauses the main loop.

Show solution

Player:

Shark 2:

The blink loop takes 10 × 0.2 = 2 seconds, so it ends right as the safe time does. The blink isn't decoration: it's how the player sees the rule that they're safe for now.

#Exercise 5: Bug hunt, the bell that hangs around

A player collects a Bell sprite. The bell should vanish to a new place the instant it's touched, with a ring. Instead, after a touch the bell sits there for about four seconds, ringing, before it moves:

Fix it so the bell moves immediately and the ring still plays in full.

Need a hint?

Two things are wrong, and both are about order and waiting. Which block makes the loop stand still, and does the bell have to finish ringing before it moves?

Show solution

play sound until done froze the loop for the whole 4-second sound, and the move came after it. Moving first takes the bell out of reach in the same pass, and start sound lets the ring play while the loop carries on.

#Exercise 6: A ball that bounces with velocity

Without using if on edge, bounce, make the Ball sprite fly around the stage using two variables, vx and vy (for this sprite only), starting at 5 and 3.5. When it reaches a side, flip vx; when it reaches the top or bottom, flip vy. Every bounce plays Boing and squashes the ball briefly, and the movement must never pause.

Need a hint?

The ball is about 44 steps wide at 100% size, so its edge meets a wall when its center is 22 steps from it: at x = ±218 and y = ±158. Flip a speed with set [vx v] to ((0) - (vx)). Put the squash in a separate script, triggered by a message, so its wait doesn't touch the loop.

Show solution

Because x and y have their own speeds, the ball can travel at any angle, and a bounce off a wall only flips the speed that points into it. That's the same idea as Pong.

#Challenge: A one-button rhythm game

Paint a round Note sprite and add the Line sprite as a hit line at y = −120. The note drops from the top at 4 steps per frame. Press space as it crosses the line:

How far the note is from the line Result
under 8 steps Perfect: +3, combo +1
8 to 19 steps Good: +1, combo +1
20 to 39 steps Miss: combo back to 0
40 or more press ignored
note falls past y = −160 unpressed Miss

After each result the note says it, and a new note starts from the top after a short random pause. Perfect hits play a higher-pitched sound than Good ones.

Need a hint?

The distance is ([abs v] of ((y position) - (-120))). Let the falling loop and the space bar script both send the note back to the top with the same message, say next note, so there's only one place that handles respawning. Why is a press at 30 steps a Miss instead of being ignored? Try spamming space without that rule.

Show solution

Note (variables score and combo for all sprites):

The space script broadcasts next note, which restarts the falling script from the top, so a judged note can't keep falling and be judged twice. That restart rule from Module 3 is doing useful work here. The say blocks have no time on purpose: the result stays on the note while it waits at the top, and say [] clears it just before the next drop. A say for 0.5 seconds would hold up the broadcast while the judged note kept falling. The Miss band between 20 and 39 steps is what makes button-mashing a bad strategy: spam the space bar and you'll usually press too early and lose your combo.

What you'll learn

  • Choose between touching, touching color, color is touching, and distance to for a collision.
  • Stop a player at walls with the move, check, undo pattern.
  • Make a sprite fall and jump with a y speed variable.
  • Keep a player on the stage and bring it back when it falls off.

Press the right arrow and your hero strolls straight through a brick wall. Scratch noticed. The moment the hero's pixels overlapped the wall, touching (Wall v)? turned true. But no script asked the question, so nothing happened.

That's how collisions work in Scratch. Sensing blocks only report that two things overlap. Your scripts decide what the overlap means: a wall pushes you back, a coin disappears, lava sends you to the start.

#Four ways a sprite can feel a touch

Scratch checks real pixels, not boxes. If the cat's tail overlaps a wall, the cat is touching the wall, even if its body is nowhere near.

Block It's true when… Use it for
touching (Wall v)? any visible pixel of this sprite overlaps the Wall sprite or one of its clones walls, enemies, pickups
touching color [ ]? this sprite overlaps that exact color, on the backdrop or on any other sprite lava or water painted into a backdrop
color [ ] is touching [ ]? one color inside this sprite overlaps another color checking only the feet or only a sword tip
distance to (Guard v) it reports a number: how many steps apart the two sprites' centers are "close enough" checks: sight range, magnets

Here are all four in one script for a player sprite:

Notice that distance to doesn't care about shapes at all. Two sprites 99 steps apart are "close" even if there's a wall between them. That makes it the right tool for "the guard notices you" and the wrong one for "you hit the guard."

⚠️ Watch out

The score jumps by 20 for one coin. touching (Coin v)? stays true for every frame the two sprites overlap, and the loop runs 30 times a second. Hide the coin (or move it away) in the same frame you count it. Hidden sprites never count as touching, so the next pass of the loop sees nothing.

#Smooth controls come from a loop, not a hat block

There are two ways to react to a key, and they feel very different to play.

Hold the right arrow with this script and the sprite moves once, pauses, then stutters along. That pause is your keyboard's repeat delay, the same one you see when you hold a letter key in a text box. And since a keyboard only repeats the last key you pressed, holding up and right together moves you in just one direction.

This version asks "is the key down right now?" 30 times a second, so movement is smooth from the first frame and every key is checked on every pass. Use the loop for anything held down (walking, steering). Keep the hat block for single taps, like pausing or switching weapons.

#Move, check, undo: walls that push back

Here's the pattern almost every Scratch game uses for solid walls:

  1. Move the player a little.
  2. Check if it's now touching a wall.
  3. If it is, move it back by the same amount.

Why doesn't the player flicker into the wall and out again? Scratch only redraws the stage at the end of each pass through the loop. By then the step back has already happened, so the overlap is never shown. The player just looks blocked.

Each direction gets its own check on purpose. If you moved right and up, then checked once and undid both, a player pressing into a wall diagonally would freeze. Checking each axis separately lets the player slide along the wall, which feels much better.

#Gravity is a speed that keeps changing

Real things don't fall at a steady speed. They speed up. To copy that, a game keeps the sprite's vertical speed in a variable and changes the speed every frame, not just the position.

Trace the first few frames in your head. y speed goes 0, −1, −2, −3, so the sprite drops 1 step, then 2, then 3. After four frames it has fallen 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10 steps, and each frame it falls faster. That curve is what makes falling look natural.

A jump is the same loop with one change: when the player presses up, set y speed to a positive number like 13. Gravity eats one point of speed per frame, so the sprite rises fast, slows to a stop at the top, and falls back down. Two numbers control the whole feel: the jump speed and the gravity. This short Python program does the exact same arithmetic as the Scratch loop, so we can plot two jumps side by side:

Higher gravity with a stronger jump feels snappy; low gravity feels floaty, like the moon. Neither is wrong, but pick on purpose.

Landing uses move, check, undo again. After change y by (y speed), if the player is touching the level, undo that move and set y speed to 0. You'll build the full version, with a rule that you can only jump from the ground, in the next lesson.

⚠️ Watch out

Falling straight through a thin platform. If y speed reaches −20 and a platform is 10 steps thick, the player can jump from above it to below it in one frame and never touch it. This is called tunneling. Cap the falling speed (if y speed < -12, set y speed to -12) and draw platforms at least 15 steps thick.

#Keeping the player on the stage

Scratch won't let a sprite leave the stage entirely. It stops the sprite with about 15 pixels still showing, which is how a player ends up stuck half-hidden at the edge, or jammed against the bottom forever.

Decide the limits yourself. The stage runs from x = −240 to 240 and y = −180 to 180, so:

The first two if blocks clamp the player: if it goes past a line, put it back on the line. The third treats falling off the bottom as a fall into a pit and sends the player back to the start. Resetting y speed matters there. Without it, the player keeps the falling speed it had and reappears already plummeting.

Check your understanding

4 questions

1A player's loop does change x by (5), then if <touching (Wall v)?> then change x by (-5). Does the player ever appear inside the wall?

  • The redraw happens at the end of the loop pass, and by then the move has already been undone.

  • Scratch draws the stage after the whole pass, so the overlap is never shown.

  • Color doesn't matter for touching (Wall v)?; it checks the Wall sprite's pixels.

Show answer

B. Scratch draws the stage after the whole pass, so the overlap is never shown.

2y speed starts at 0. Each frame runs change [y speed v] by (-1) then change y by (y speed). How far has the sprite fallen after 4 frames?

  • That would be a steady speed of 1. Here the speed grows every frame.

  • It falls 1, then 2, then 3, then 4 steps: 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10.

  • That's 4 × 4, as if it fell 4 steps every frame from the start.

Show answer

B. It falls 1, then 2, then 3, then 4 steps: 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10.

3The score goes up by about 15 every time the player grabs one coin. What's the best fix?

  • The loop isn't the problem; the overlap lasts several frames.

  • A hidden sprite never counts as touching, so the next frames don't add more.

  • Distance also stays small for several frames, so the score would still jump.

Show answer

B. A hidden sprite never counts as touching, so the next frames don't add more.

4A guard should shout when the player comes within 120 steps, even around corners. Which block fits?

  • That only fires when pixels actually overlap.

  • The player isn't one fixed color, and this is about range, not overlap.

  • It reports how far apart the centers are, so < (120) is a sight range.

Show answer

C. It reports how far apart the centers are, so < (120) is a sight range.

Key takeaways

  • Sensing blocks report overlaps; your script decides what they mean.
  • Use key pressed? inside a forever loop for smooth, held-down movement.
  • Move, check, undo, once per direction, makes walls solid and lets players slide along them.
  • Gravity changes the speed every frame, and the speed changes the position.
  • Clamp the player's x position and treat falling below the stage as a reset, with y speed set back to 0.

#Further reading

  • Touching ()? on the Scratch Wiki (opens in a new tab): how pixel collisions work, including the rule about hidden sprites.
  • Simulating Gravity on the Scratch Wiki (opens in a new tab): more ways to model falling, with example scripts.
  • How to Go Off the Screen Edge (opens in a new tab): what sprite fencing is and why the 15-pixel margin exists.

What you'll learn

  • Paint a level as one sprite and use it for every floor, wall, and ceiling check.
  • Combine gravity, landing, and walls with the move, check, undo pattern.
  • Allow jumping only when the player is standing on something.
  • Respawn the player after a fall and end the game when it reaches the goal.

You're building a small platformer called Crystal Climb. A square hero named Pip starts on the left, jumps up three platforms, clears a short wall and a pit, and grabs a crystal at the top right. Here's the level on the Scratch stage grid, with each character standing for 10 steps across and 30 steps up:

When you finish, Pip will walk smoothly, fall faster and faster, land on any platform, stop at walls, bump into ceilings, and reappear at the start after falling into the pit. Every one of those behaviors comes from one sprite, Level, and one pattern: move, check, undo.

#Step 1: Paint the level and the hero

Start a new project at scratch.mit.edu (opens in a new tab) and delete the cat.

  1. Hover over Choose a Sprite and click the paintbrush (Paint). Name the sprite Level.
  2. With the Rectangle tool and a filled color, draw the ground, the three platforms, and the wall from the map. Make every piece at least 20 steps thick. Use one color for all of them.
  3. Paint a second sprite, a filled square a little taller than a platform is thick. Name it Pip. Add eyes if you like, but keep the outline a plain square so it never snags on corners.
  4. From the sprite library, add Crystal and drag it onto the top-right platform. Set its size to about 50.

The paint canvas is the same size as the stage, so give the level a script that parks it in the middle, where what you painted lines up with where it appears:

Click the green flag. Nothing moves yet, but the level should sit exactly where you drew it.

#Step 2: Walk left and right

Select Pip. Make two variables with For this sprite only selected: y speed and on ground. Then start Pip's main script:

Run it. Pip glides left and right, floating in the air and passing through the wall like a ghost. Both problems are next.

#Step 3: Add gravity

Inside the forever loop, after the arrow keys, add the falling code from the Notes. Also set y speed to 0 right after the go to at the top, so every game starts from rest.

Run it. Pip falls straight through the ground and ends up wedged against the bottom of the stage. Scratch's fencing is the only thing stopping it, and fencing isn't a floor.

#Step 4: Land on the level

After change y by (y speed), check for the level and undo the fall if Pip went into it:

(0) - (y speed) is the opposite of the move Pip just made. If it fell 9 steps, this moves it up 9.

Run it. Pip drops and stops on the ground. Watch closely after a long fall: Pip stops a few steps above the ground, then settles the rest of the way over the next few frames. The undo puts Pip back where it was before the last move, which can leave a small gap. It's barely visible, and Module 6 has a pixel-perfect fix using a custom block.

#Step 5: Jump, but only from the ground

Try the obvious version first. Add this at the end of the loop:

Run it and hold the up arrow. Pip flies off the top of the stage, because every frame of holding up resets the speed to 13, even mid-air. The game needs to remember whether Pip is standing on something.

Remove that if and rebuild the landing part so it records that fact:

on ground is reset to 0 every frame and only becomes 1 if Pip was moving down when it hit the level. Standing still counts, because gravity tugs Pip 1 step into the floor every frame and the undo lifts it back out.

Run it. One press of up gives one jump, about 78 steps high. Holding up just jumps again each time Pip lands.

#Step 6: Solid walls and ceilings

Walk Pip into the short wall. It passes right through, because only the vertical move is checked. Give each arrow key its own undo:

Now jump while standing under platform B. Pip's head hits the bottom of the platform and it falls back down. You didn't write any ceiling code: the landing check from Step 5 already undoes the move and stops the speed. The y speed < 0 test is what keeps a head bump from counting as standing, so Pip can't jump again from the underside of a platform.

#Step 7: Pits, edges, and a speed limit

Three last rules go at the end of the loop. They cap the falling speed so Pip can't tunnel through a platform, keep Pip on the stage left to right, and send Pip home after a fall into the pit.

The speed cap belongs just before change y by (y speed) in the finished script, so the limit applies to the move that's about to happen. Drop Pip into the pit to check that it reappears at the start, standing still.

#Step 8: Reach the crystal

The crystal decides when the game is won. It waits until Pip touches it, then tells everyone:

Pip listens and freezes in place:

stop [other scripts in sprite v] ends Pip's forever loop but leaves this script running, so Pip can still talk.

#The finished scripts

Here is Pip's whole main script with every step in place. The Level and Crystal scripts are exactly as above.

If a jump you painted turns out to be impossible, move the platform, not the code. The jump is about 78 steps high and carries Pip about 100 steps sideways, so keep each platform within about 60 steps up and 60 steps across from the one before.

Check your understanding

3 questions

1Why does the script only set on ground to 1 when y speed is less than 0?

  • The check doesn't change any speed; it only decides whether a jump is allowed.

  • A head bump also touches the level. Without the test, Pip could jump again from the underside of a platform.

  • It's positive while Pip rises, which is exactly the case the test filters out.

Show answer

B. A head bump also touches the level. Without the test, Pip could jump again from the underside of a platform.

2You remove the y speed < -12 cap and make a very high drop onto a 10-step-thick platform. What can happen?

  • At high speed Pip can jump from above the platform to below it in one frame, so touching is never true.

  • Nothing in the script makes a bounce; the undo just stops the fall.

  • Scratch never complains; the collision silently gets missed.

Show answer

A. At high speed Pip can jump from above the platform to below it in one frame, so touching is never true.

3When Pip falls into the pit, the script runs go to x: (-200) y: (-90). What goes wrong if you forget set [y speed v] to (0) after it?

  • Variables keep their values until a script changes them.

  • y speed is still about −12, so the first frame after respawning moves Pip 12 steps down.

  • Jumping depends on on ground, which still works after landing.

Show answer

B. y speed is still about −12, so the first frame after respawning moves Pip 12 steps down.

Key takeaways

  • Painting every solid thing into one Level sprite means one touching (Level v)? check covers floors, walls, and ceilings.
  • Undo each axis separately: x right after the arrow keys, y right after gravity.
  • A flag variable like on ground, reset every frame, is how a game remembers what happened this frame.
  • Speed caps, clamps, and resets are small rules that stop whole families of bugs.

#Ideas to extend it

  • Coyote time. Let Pip jump for a few frames after walking off a ledge. Count frames since Pip was last on the ground and allow a jump if the count is under 4.
  • Short hops. If the player lets go of up while y speed is still above 4, set it to 4. Tapping gives a small hop and holding gives a full jump.
  • Lava. Paint a red strip into a separate Lava sprite and send Pip home when it touches it.
  • A second level. Paint a new costume for Level and switch to it when the crystal is found. Module 7 turns this into a proper level system.

#Further reading

  • How to Make a Basic Platformer (opens in a new tab): the Scratch Wiki's own version, useful for comparing approaches.
  • Velocity on the Scratch Wiki (opens in a new tab): why storing speed in a variable makes motion feel real.

What you'll learn

  • Pick the right sensing block for hazards, pickups, and sight ranges.
  • Make a touch count exactly once.
  • Run two scripts in one sprite: one that moves, one that watches.
  • Track a player's state across frames to build a double jump.

Most exercises add to Crystal Climb from the Build-along, so open that project first. If you're signed in, File › Save as a copy keeps the original untouched.

#Warm-up: name the block

For each situation, decide which sensing block you'd use before you check the answer: touching (sprite)?, touching color?, color is touching color?, or distance to.

  1. A bat swoops into the player.
  2. The player's sword tip (painted bright yellow) hits a red balloon.
  3. A dog starts barking when the player gets near.
  4. The player steps in a puddle painted into the backdrop.
Show solution
  1. touching (Bat v)?, because both are sprites and you care about real overlap.
  2. color [yellow] is touching [red]?, run by the player sprite, so only the sword tip counts and a bump with your elbow doesn't.
  3. distance to (Player v), compared with a number like 150. Nearness isn't overlap.
  4. touching color [puddle blue]?, since the puddle isn't a sprite at all.

#Exercise 1: Spikes that send you home

Paint a new sprite called Spikes (a row of triangles) and put it on platform B. When Pip touches the spikes, it should go back to the start, stop moving, and add 1 to a falls variable that the game shows on the stage. Falling into the pit should also count as a fall.

Need a hint?

You already have respawn code for the pit. Turn its condition into "fell below −160 or touching Spikes". The count goes up only once because Pip is teleported away in the same frame, so the next frame isn't touching anything.

Show solution

Replace the pit check at the end of Pip's loop, and add set [falls v] to (0) near the top of the script.

Make falls For all sprites so its monitor reads "falls" on the stage and other sprites can read it later.

#Exercise 2: Count the coin once

Here's a coin script with a bug. Paint a small yellow circle called Coin, give it this script, and walk Pip through it.

Fix it so each touch adds exactly 1, the coin disappears, and it comes back 2 seconds later somewhere random in the top half of the stage.

Need a hint?

The score climbs for every frame of overlap. What's the quickest way to make touching stop being true?

Show solution

hide is the important line. A hidden sprite never counts as touching, so the loop can't see Pip again until the coin reappears.

#Exercise 3: A guard who sees you coming

Add the library sprite Knight (or any character) on the right-hand ground, at about size 50. It should patrol back and forth forever. When Pip comes within 120 steps, the knight says "Halt!" and turns to face Pip. When Pip leaves that range, the knight stops talking.

Need a hint?

Use two scripts in the knight: one that only patrols with glide, and one that only watches with distance to. Both start with the green flag and run at the same time.

Show solution

say [] with nothing in it clears the speech bubble. Set the knight's rotation style to left-right (in the sprite's direction settings, or with set rotation style [left-right v]) so pointing at Pip flips it instead of tipping it over.

#Exercise 4: A bounce pad

Add the library sprite Trampoline on the right-hand ground. When Pip lands on it, Pip should shoot upward much higher than a normal jump.

Need a hint?

Check right after change y by (y speed) and before the Level landing check, which sets y speed to 0. "Lands on" means touching the trampoline while moving down.

Show solution

The y speed < 0 part matters: without it, Pip would be launched again on the way up while still overlapping the pad. Gravity takes away 1 per frame, so a speed of 20 climbs 19 + 18 + … + 1 = 190 steps.

#Exercise 5: Slide along walls in a top-down game

Start a new project with the library sprite Beetle at size 40 and a Walls sprite painted as a simple room with a few inside walls. Make the beetle move in all four directions with the arrow keys at 3 steps per frame, stopping at walls. Then test it: hold right and up together against a wall on the right. The beetle should slide up along the wall, not freeze.

Need a hint?

Four if key pressed? blocks, each with its own move and its own undo. If you move on both axes and check once, a diagonal push freezes the beetle.

Show solution

Pressing right into the wall gets undone, but the separate up move doesn't touch anything, so it stays. Slide along walls comes for free. If the beetle catches on corners, its costume is too detailed; try a smaller size.

#Exercise 6: Double jump

Let Pip jump once more while in the air. Each press of the up arrow gives one jump, holding it down doesn't use up both jumps, and landing restores both.

Need a hint?

You need two new variables. jumps left replaces on ground: set it to 2 whenever Pip lands. up held remembers whether the up arrow was already down last frame, so a jump only happens on a new press. The diagram below shows the states.

Show solution

In the landing check, replace set [on ground v] to (1) with set [jumps left v] to (2), and delete set [on ground v] to (0). Then replace the old jump if with this:

On the first frame of a press, up held is still 0, so the jump fires. Every frame after that, up held is 1, so holding the key does nothing more. Letting go sets it back to 0, ready for the next press. One quirk: walking off a ledge leaves both jumps unused, so Pip gets two air jumps. If you don't want that, give the landing check an else: when Pip isn't touching the level and jumps left is 2, set it to 1.

#Challenge: momentum and ice

Right now Pip starts and stops instantly. Give it momentum: add an x speed variable. The arrow keys change x speed by 1 (or −1), every frame multiplies it by 0.8 for friction, and Pip moves by x speed with the usual undo. Then paint one platform light blue in the Level costume and make it icy: on ice, Pip should be slow to speed up and slow to stop.

Need a hint?

After undoing a horizontal move into a wall, set x speed to 0, or Pip will keep pressing into it. For ice, the tricky part is when to check. Pip only overlaps the floor right after change y by (y speed) and before the undo, so test touching color there and store the answer in a variable.

Show solution

Replace the two arrow-key if blocks at the top of Pip's loop with this:

Inside the vertical landing check, before the undo, add:

Use the color picker's eyedropper to choose the exact blue from your costume. On normal ground, holding a key settles at a top speed of 4 steps per frame, the same as before, and Pip stops almost at once. On ice, Pip speeds up slowly to a top speed of 6 and takes about two seconds to slide to a stop. Ice needs both changes: low friction alone (0.97 with a grip of 1) gives a top speed above 30, and Pip rockets off the stage.

m6-l1.html:
What you'll learn

  • Create, control, and delete clones, and explain what a clone copies from its parent.
  • Give each clone its own values with For this sprite only variables.
  • Find and fix the clone explosion bug.
  • Build a custom block with inputs, and know when to tick Run without screen refresh.
  • Store and read many values with a list.

A student's ghost game had one rule: press space, get a ghost. The first press made 1 ghost. The second made the count 3. Then 7, then 15. By the sixth press there were 63 ghosts and the game had slowed to a crawl. Nothing in the script said "double". By the end of this page you'll know exactly why it happened, and the one-line fix.

#Clones: one sprite, many copies

A clone is a copy of a sprite that exists only while the project runs. You write the scripts once, and every copy runs them on its own. Three blocks from Control do the work:

At the moment it's made, a clone copies everything about its parent: position, direction, costume, size, effects, whether it's showing, and the values of its variables. After that it's independent. Clones don't appear in the sprite list, and they all disappear when you click the stop sign or the green flag.

Here's a common setup: the original sprite hides and acts as a factory, and the clones do the work.

The factory moves to a random height before each create clone, so every clone starts at a different spot. Each clone shows itself (it was born hidden, like its parent), flies across, and deletes itself at the far edge. That last step matters: Scratch allows at most 300 clones at once, and clones you forget to delete keep counting toward the limit until the game stops making new ones.

#Giving each clone its own memory

Make a variable with For this sprite only selected and every clone gets its own copy. Change it in one clone and the others don't notice. A variable made For all sprites is a single shared box: if each clone sets speed, they all end up using whichever value was set last.

With a For this sprite only speed, six clones fly at six different speeds. Switch it to For all sprites and they all fly at the same speed.

#Why 1 ghost became 63

Clones run every script in their sprite that starts with a hat block, except green flag scripts (those already ran before the clone existed). That includes key presses and broadcasts. So this script runs in the original and in every clone:

Press 1: the original makes 1 clone. Press 2: the original and that clone each make one, so now there are 3. Press 3: four sprites each make one, giving 7. After n presses there are 2ⁿ − 1 clones, which is 63 after six presses.

The fix is to make sure only one sprite does the spawning. Either move the key script to a sprite that's never cloned, using create clone of (Ghost v) from there, or put the spawning in a green flag loop, which clones never run:

#My Blocks: give a chunk of code a name

Open the pink My Blocks category and click Make a Block. Type a name, and use Add an input number or text (or Add an input boolean) for anything that changes from one use to the next. Click OK and a define hat appears in the code area. Whatever you snap under it runs every time the block is used.

The inputs height and bat speed are like variables that only exist inside the definition. Notice the trick in the middle: the original sets its own speed, then creates a clone, and the clone keeps a copy of that value. Three calls, three bats, three different speeds.

A custom block belongs to the sprite it was made in. Other sprites can't see it. To reuse one elsewhere, drag the define script onto another sprite in the sprite list to copy it there.

#Run without screen refresh: finish a loop in one frame

Remember the small gap when Pip landed in Module 5? The precise fix is to push Pip up one step at a time until it's just out of the floor:

Normally, each pass of a loop that moves a sprite waits for the screen to redraw. If Pip lands 10 steps deep, this loop takes 10 frames: you see Pip sink into the floor and climb back out while the rest of its script waits. Tick Run without screen refresh in the Make a Block window and the whole loop finishes before the next redraw. Pip lands exactly on the surface, every time. (To change the setting later, right-click the define block and choose Edit.)

Use it for blocks that calculate or position things, like collision fixes or drawing a grid. Never use it for anything the player should watch happen.

⚠️ Watch out

A wait or forever inside a no-refresh block freezes the project. Scratch tries to finish the whole block before drawing, so a glide, a wait (1) seconds, or an endless loop inside it makes the stage lock up instead of animating. If your game suddenly freezes after you tick the box, look for a wait or a loop that never ends.

#Lists: one name, many values

A variable holds one value. A list holds as many as you like, numbered from 1. Make one with Make a List in the Variables category.

⚠️ Watch out

The list gets longer every time you click the green flag. Lists keep their contents when the project stops, and they're saved with it. Without delete all of [heights v] at the start, the second run adds three more items, and the third adds three more. Clear a list before you fill it.

A spark that hits a ghost makes it fade away and scores a point. A ghost that slips past costs a life, and losing three ends the game.

m7-l1.html:
What you'll learn

  • Map a whole game as states and arrows before writing its broadcasts.
  • Use broadcast and wait so a new level is fully set up before play begins.
  • Store each level's settings in lists, one item per level.
  • Compare difficulty curves and design one with rests.
  • Adjust difficulty between rounds based on how the player did, within safe limits.

Hand Ghost Patrol to a friend and watch. For the first minute they lean in. By minute three they're dodging on autopilot, because minute three is exactly as hard as minute one. The score climbs, but nothing else about the game changes.

Good games have a shape. There's a beginning that tells you what's going on, a middle that pushes harder and then lets you breathe, and an ending you can win or lose. None of that needs new blocks. It needs a plan for when things happen, and that's what this lesson is about.

#Map every state before you code

In Module 3 you kept a game's mode in a state variable and checked it before reacting to keys. A multi-level game has more states than a single round, and the arrows between them multiply fast. So draw the whole map first: every box is a state, and every arrow is a broadcast you'll have to write.

Notice the loop between Playing and WaveCleared. The same two states repeat once per wave, which means the code for them should be written once and fed different numbers each time. That's the idea behind the next two sections.

Stories fit the same picture. Each scene is a state and each choice is an arrow. "The left door leads to the crypt, the right door to the tower" is one box with two arrows leaving it, and a player's typed answer decides which arrow to follow.

#Set up the level, then start playing

Starting a new level means several sprites must change at once: the level costume switches, the player moves to the new start point, the old enemies disappear. If the player starts moving before the new costume appears, it can begin the level inside a wall.

Module 3's broadcast and wait is the tool for this. Split every level change into two messages: one that gets everything ready, sent with and wait, and one that starts the action.

Everything that must be ready goes in load level scripts. Everything that moves goes in begin play scripts. Plain broadcast doesn't wait, so the scripts that come next run alongside the ones it started, in an order you don't control.

#Levels are rows of settings

You could write a separate script for every level, but then five levels means five copies of the same code. Instead, write the code once and keep what changes between levels in lists, one item per level:

Wave wave size spawn gap (seconds)
1 5 1.8
2 7 1.5
3 9 1.2
4 7 1.4
5 12 0.9

Each list is one column of this table, and the wave number picks the row:

Adding wave 6 is now two add blocks, not a new script. For a platformer, the level number can also pick the costume: switch costume to (level) with a number selects the costume in that position, so costume 3 is level 3.

#Shape the difficulty curve

How hard each level is, plotted in order, is the game's difficulty curve. Three common shapes:

The flat curve is what Ghost Patrol has now: easy to learn, boring by wave 3. The steady ramp never lets up, so players get tired and start losing on wave 6 without knowing why. The ramp with rests climbs, then drops for one easier wave (4 and 7) before climbing higher. That dip gives players a moment to feel how much better they've become, and it makes the next jump feel fair. Music and movies use the same tension-then-release shape.

Look at the table above again: wave 4 is a rest.

#Let the game adapt to the player

A fixed curve is a guess about a typical player. Your best friend and your little cousin aren't typical. Adaptive difficulty measures how the player is doing and nudges the challenge to match.

The recipe has three parts: measure something, adjust a difficulty number by a small step, and clamp it so it can't run away.

A perfect wave makes the next one a little faster, a rough wave makes it a little slower, and one lost life changes nothing. The ghost factory adds bonus to each ghost's speed.

Two rules keep it from feeling unfair. Adjust between rounds, never in the middle, so the player can't see the game moving the goalposts. And keep the steps small: half a step of speed is something players feel without noticing why.

⚠️ Watch out

A difficulty number that goes too far breaks the game. If bonus can reach −3 and a ghost's base speed is 1, its speed becomes −2 and it drifts backward, off the right edge, and the wave never ends. Clamp the difficulty number, and clamp anything you calculate from it (like a minimum ghost speed of 0.5).

⚠️ Watch out

Last level's enemies are still flying. Clones don't disappear when the level changes, and they hear load level too, so a factory that spawns on load level gets help from every old clone. Make delete this clone the first block of the factory's load level script. Each old clone runs it and vanishes; in the original sprite the block does nothing, so the original carries on and spawns the new level's enemies.

Check your understanding

4 questions

1The Stage runs broadcast (load level v) (without "and wait") and then broadcast (begin play v). What can go wrong?

  • They arrive in order, but plain broadcast doesn't wait for the first message's scripts to finish.

  • begin play is sent while the load level scripts are still running, so the player might start inside a wall.

  • A different message doesn't stop the first message's scripts.

Show answer

B. begin play is sent while the load level scripts are still running, so the player might start inside a wall.

2Using the table above, what does item (wave) of [spawn gap v] report during wave 3?

  • That's item (3) of [wave size v], the other list.

  • Wave 3 is row 3, and the third item of spawn gap is 1.2.

  • The wave number picks the item; it isn't the item itself.

Show answer

B. Wave 3 is row 3, and the third item of spawn gap is 1.2.

3A playtester loses 3 lives in wave 2. Using adapt difficulty above, starting from bonus = 0, what happens to the next wave?

  • More than one life lost subtracts 0.5 from bonus.

  • The change is one step of 0.5, however badly the wave went.

  • The block runs after every wave, not just at game over.

Show answer

A. More than one life lost subtracts 0.5 from bonus.

4Why does the ramp with rests drop at waves 4 and 7?

  • The number of waves is the same in every curve.

  • An easier wave after a hard one feels like relief, and it makes the next climb feel fair.

  • The dips are on purpose; they're the whole point of the design.

Show answer

B. An easier wave after a hard one feels like relief, and it makes the next climb feel fair.

Key takeaways

  • Draw your game's states first; every arrow becomes one broadcast.
  • Clear old clones at the start of every level load.
  • broadcast and wait makes a level fully ready before anything starts moving.
  • Store what changes between levels in lists, one item per level, and write the level code once.
  • Climb, rest, climb higher. Adapt between rounds in small, clamped steps.

#Further reading

  • Broadcast on the Scratch Wiki (opens in a new tab): how messages work, including broadcast and wait.
  • Dynamic game difficulty balancing (opens in a new tab): how commercial games adjust difficulty, with real examples.
  • Flow (psychology) (opens in a new tab): the idea that people enjoy tasks most when the challenge matches their skill.

  • Speed isn't the reason; both versions finish instantly.

  • If one list got an extra item, every later wave would read the wrong gap. One block per row makes that mistake impossible.

  • Any script can add to a list.

Show answer

B. If one list got an extra item, every later wave would read the wrong gap. One block per row makes that mistake impossible.

2Why does the spawn block set any speed below 0.5 back up to 0.5?

  • It only affects the slowest ghosts, when bonus is low.

  • ghosts left only reaches 0 when every ghost is hit or escapes; a frozen ghost does neither.

  • change x by (0.3) works fine; the floor is about keeping the game finishable.

Show answer

B. ghosts left only reaches 0 when every ghost is hit or escapes; a frozen ghost does neither.

3Why does adapt difficulty run between waves instead of every second during play?

  • Between waves the change feels like the next level, not like the game reacting to every mistake.

  • Custom blocks can run anywhere; this is a design choice.

  • It's readable any time; it's reset at the start of each wave so it measures one wave.

Show answer

A. Between waves the change feels like the next level, not like the game reacting to every mistake.

Key takeaways

  • One Stage script that walks through the states is easier to follow than many scripts guessing what's happening.
  • A custom block per row keeps parallel lists in step.
  • Count what's left (ghosts left) so the game knows exactly when a wave is done.
  • Every number that adapts needs a clamp, and so does anything calculated from it.
  • Playtest with the hidden variables showing, then hide them.

#Ideas to extend it

  • A boss wave. Add a sixth wave with one huge, slow ghost that takes 10 hits (combine with the tough ghost challenge from Module 6).
  • Play again. Instead of stop [all v], wait for space and loop back to the title. Remember that set up game has to run again.
  • Story between waves. Use the wave cleared message to tell one more line of the story each time.
  • Show the adaptation. When bonus goes up, flash the backdrop with the brightness effect so skilled players know the game noticed.

#Further reading

  • Game Projects on the Scratch Wiki (opens in a new tab): a tour of game types with tips for each, useful for planning your capstone.

What you'll learn

  • Clear out old clones when a new level loads.
  • Branch a story on the player's answer and handle answers you didn't expect.
  • Read a difficulty curve from a list and write one with rests.
  • Adapt difficulty from a streak, with limits.
  • Load levels from lists using broadcast and wait.

Exercises 1, 2, 4, and 6 start from new projects. Exercise 3 uses Ghost Patrol, and Exercise 5 and the challenge use Crystal Climb.

#Warm-up: draw the states

Crystal Climb is getting three levels in Exercise 5. On paper, draw its states as boxes and its messages as arrows: title, playing a level, level complete, and won. What message sends the game from "level complete" back to "playing"?

Show solution

Title → Playing (space pressed) → LevelComplete (crystal found) → Playing (load level, then begin play) → … → Won (crystal found on level 3). The arrow back to Playing is really two messages in a row: load level with and wait, then begin play. Drawing it first tells you both broadcasts you'll need.

#Exercise 1: Too many bats on level 2

A friend's platformer spawns bats with this script. The list bat count holds 2, 3, 4 (one item per level). Level 1 has 2 bats, as planned. Before you build it, predict how many bats are flying on level 2. Then fix it so level 2 has exactly 3.

Need a hint?

On level 2, which sprites hear load level? The hidden original does, and so does every clone left over from level 1. What does each of them do with the message?

Show solution

Level 2 has 11 bats. The original and the two old clones all run the script, and each makes 3 copies of itself: 3 × 3 = 9 new bats, plus the 2 old ones still flying.

Every old clone hits delete this clone and disappears before it can spawn anything. In the original sprite that block does nothing, so the original moves on to the loop and makes exactly 3.

#Exercise 2: Two doors, any answer

Write a tiny story. A narrator says "You wake in a dark hall. Two doors stand ahead." and then asks the player to type left or right. Left switches to one backdrop and says a line about a crypt; right switches to another and says a line about a tower. If the player types anything else, such as lfet or the middle one, ask again.

Need a hint?

Save the answer in a variable and use repeat until with an or of the two good answers. Scratch's = ignores capital letters, so LEFT already counts as left.

Show solution

Without the loop, an if/else sends every typo through the else door, so "lfet" would take the player to the tower. The loop makes sure the if only ever sees a real choice. Use any two backdrops you like.

#Exercise 3: Read a curve, then write one

Here are three wave size lists for an 8-wave game. Which one is flat, which is a steady ramp, and which ramps with rests?

Then write 8 add wave lines for Ghost Patrol's set up game block with rests at waves 4 and 7 and the hardest wave last. Remember that spawn gap matters too: a rest can be fewer ghosts, a longer gap, or both.

Need a hint?

A rest is a wave that's easier than the one before it. Look for the places where the numbers go down.

Show solution

A is the steady ramp, B is flat, and C ramps with rests (it dips at waves 4 and 7). One possible 8-wave design:

Each rest is still harder than the start of the previous climb (wave 4 is harder than wave 1, and wave 7 is harder than wave 4), so the game keeps moving forward. Because the Stage's wave loop uses length of [wave size v], it plays all 8 waves without any other change.

#Exercise 4: A quiz that adapts

Make a 10-question addition quiz. Each question adds two random numbers from 1 to top, where top starts at 10. Two right answers in a row raise top by 5 (up to 50). A wrong answer lowers it by 5 (down to 5) and resets the streak. At the end, say the score out of 10.

Need a hint?

You need top, streak, score, and two variables a and b for the numbers. Build the question with nested join blocks. Clamp top after every question, not just when it changes.

Show solution

This is the same measure, step, clamp recipe as adapt difficulty, applied every question instead of every wave. Questions are short enough that adapting this often still feels fair.

#Exercise 5: Three levels for Crystal Climb

Paint two more costumes for the Level sprite (costumes 2 and 3) with different platform layouts. Store each level's start point and crystal position in four lists, start x, start y, crystal x, and crystal y, one item per level. Reaching the crystal on levels 1 and 2 loads the next level; reaching it on level 3 wins. Falling into a pit sends Pip back to this level's start.

Need a hint?

Use two messages, as in the Notes. load level (sent with and wait) switches the costume, moves the crystal, and places Pip. begin play starts Pip's movement loop and the crystal's wait until. The diagram below shows the order.

Show solution

Stage (fill the lists with your own numbers):

Level: when I receive [load level v] → switch costume to (level).

Crystal: replace its old green flag script with these two.

Pip: change the main script's hat from when green flag clicked to when I receive [begin play v], delete the opening go to, and replace the old crystal found script with these:

stop [other scripts in sprite v] ends the old movement loop, so Pip stands still while the level changes, and begin play starts the loop fresh. Inside the main loop, the pit respawn uses the same two item blocks instead of (−200, −90).

#Exercise 6: A rival who rubber-bands

Make a two-sprite race, like the Module 3 race but with the computer as your opponent. The player's sprite moves 6 steps right each time you press the right arrow. A rival sprite moves on its own, and its speed depends on the gap: 2 + (player x − rival x) / 40, kept between 1 and 5. When it's far behind it speeds up, and when it's far ahead it eases off. The first to pass x = 200 wins.

Need a hint?

Read the player's position from the rival's script with the sensing block ([x position v] of (Player v)). Calculate the speed, clamp it, then move.

Show solution

The player's sprite needs its own finish check:

The race stays close whatever the player's skill, which is the point of rubber-banding. Racing games use it to keep the pack together. Push the cap too high, though, and good players feel cheated when a rival they lapped catches up out of nowhere.

#Challenge: a helping hand after three falls

In Crystal Climb, count falls on the current level. After 3 falls on the same level, give the player an extra platform that makes the hardest jump easier, and have Pip say "Here's a hand." Moving to the next level resets the count and removes the help.

Need a hint?

Paint costumes 4, 5, and 6 as copies of levels 1, 2, and 3 with one extra platform each. Then the assisted version of a level is just switch costume to ((level) + (3)). Reset the count in load level. Put each helper platform away from the start point so it never appears on top of Pip.

Show solution

In Pip's pit respawn, add one line and a check:

Add set [falls here v] to (0) to Pip's load level script. Then in the Level sprite:

load level already switches back to (level), so the help disappears on the next level. Testing tip: show the falls here monitor and fall in on purpose three times to see the switch happen. Note that say … for (2) seconds pauses Pip's loop for two seconds; use say without a time and clear it later if that bothers you.

m8-l1.html:
What you'll learn

  • List the eight things your capstone game must include.
  • Choose a game idea that fits your time and skills.
  • Fill in a one-page plan covering controls, states, sprites, variables, lists, and messages.
  • Split features into must-have, nice-to-have, and only-if-time.

Most unfinished Scratch games die the same way. There's a gorgeous title screen, a detailed plan for twenty levels, and a player sprite that still can't jump properly. Three weeks later the project hasn't been opened.

A three-level game that works beats a twenty-level game that doesn't. This capstone asks for something small and complete, and the plan you make today is what keeps it small.

#The brief

Build a game in Scratch with at least three levels (or waves, rounds, or chapters). It must have all eight of these:

# Requirement What it looks like Where you learned it
1 Start and end states A title screen, plus a win ending and a lose ending Modules 3 and 7
2 Instructions Controls and goal on the title screen or in a story intro Module 7
3 Progress the player can see Level number, score, lives, or a timer on screen Module 3
4 Collisions that matter Walls, hazards, pickups, or hits that change the game Module 5
5 Sound or animation Costume animation, effects, or sounds for actions Modules 2 and 3
6 A custom block At least one My Block you wrote and use Module 6
7 Clones At least one sprite that makes and deletes clones Module 6
8 Rising or adaptive difficulty Levels that get harder, difficulty that reacts to the player, or both Module 7

You can reuse any project from this course as a starting point. Remixing your own Crystal Climb or Ghost Patrol is allowed, as long as the finished game goes well beyond the Build-along version.

#Five ideas, from gentle to ambitious

Pick one, or invent your own at a similar size. Stars show roughly how much new code you'll need.

Crystal Climb: Three Caves ★. Extend your Module 5 platformer into three levels with the level system from Module 7's Practice. Add bat clones that patrol each cave, more of them on each level, and a helper platform after three falls. The next lesson builds this one as its worked example, so it's the safest choice.

Ghost Patrol: Siege ★. Take the Module 7 version further: a boss wave, a power-up that drops from defeated ghosts (as clones), tough ghosts, and the top-5 high-score table from Module 6.

Lantern Dive ★★. A top-down underwater game. A diver swims in four directions with wall sliding (Module 5 Practice) through a cave, collecting pearl clones before the oxygen timer runs out. Each level is deeper: a darker backdrop, less oxygen, and faster jellyfish clones drifting across the path.

Spell Duel ★★. A story-driven quiz battle. Each level is a new opponent with a short scene before the fight. Right answers cast a spell (a particle burst custom block) that drains the opponent's power; wrong answers let the opponent strike back. Question difficulty adapts like the Module 7 quiz.

Haunted Path ★★★. A small tower defense game. Ghosts follow a winding path whose corners are stored in two lists (path x and path y), and each clone remembers which corner it's heading for. Click to place lantern clones that cost coins and zap nearby ghosts using distance to. Waves come from lists.

💡 Tip

Choose the idea where you already know how to build the core action, the thing the player does every second. If you can't picture the script for "the diver swims" or "the lantern zaps a ghost," pick a smaller idea.

#Fill in a one-page plan

Copy this into a document or onto paper and fill in every line. Leaving a line blank is fine; leaving it blank by accident is how games stall in week two.

Here's the start of a filled-in plan for Lantern Dive, so you can see the level of detail that helps:

#Draw the states

Every plan should include the state diagram, because each arrow becomes a broadcast you'll have to write. Most multi-level games fit this shape; rename the boxes for yours.

#Cut it down to a game you'll finish

Sort every feature into three groups before you write any code.

  • Must have: the eight requirements, plus the one action that makes your game your game. If any of these is missing, it isn't done.
  • Nice to have: things that make it better but that the game works without, like a high-score table or a fourth level.
  • Only if time: everything else. Most of these won't happen, and that's fine.

A good test: could you explain your must-have list to a friend in 30 seconds? If it takes longer, move something down a group.

⚠️ Watch out

Art first, code later is a trap. It's tempting to spend the first session drawing ten perfect costumes. Use rough rectangles and library sprites until the game works, then swap in good art. If you change your mind about the design, you've lost five minutes of scribbles instead of an afternoon of drawing.

#Check the plan before you build

Read your plan once more and make sure you can answer yes to all of these:

  1. Does every one of the eight requirements show up somewhere in the plan?
  2. Do your levels differ by data (numbers in lists, costumes) rather than by copies of whole scripts?
  3. Does every clone have a line saying when it's deleted?
  4. Does every variable have a starting value that the green flag sets?
  5. Is the must-have list short enough that you could finish it in about half your available time?

If a "no" comes up, fix the plan now. It's much cheaper to change a sentence than a script.

Key takeaways

  • The brief has eight requirements; map each one to a part of your game before you start.
  • Pick an idea whose core action you already know how to build.
  • A one-page plan with sprites, variables, lists, messages, and states saves hours of rework.
  • Levels should differ by data, not by copied scripts.
  • Must have, nice to have, only if time: build the first group completely before touching the second.

#Further reading

  • Scratch Ideas (opens in a new tab): official tutorials and starter projects, handy for features like animation and sound.
  • Game Projects on the Scratch Wiki (opens in a new tab): common game genres and what each one usually needs.

m8-l2.html:
What you'll learn

  • Start from a skeleton whose states and messages work before any gameplay exists.
  • Build in six milestones, each one playable and tested before the next.
  • Load levels with load level and begin play, and clear old clones safely.
  • Keep a saved version after every milestone.

The safest way to build a game is to keep it playable the whole time. Each milestone below ends with a game that runs from the title screen to an ending, even if early versions are mostly rectangles. If you run out of time, you hand in the last milestone that worked, not a half-finished pile of scripts.

The worked example is Crystal Climb: Three Caves, the platformer from Module 5 grown into a full game. If you chose a different idea, follow the same milestones and use the table at the end to translate each part.

💡 Tip

Save a version at the end of every milestone, with the milestone number in the project title ("Three Caves m3"). If you're signed in, File › Save as a copy does this; offline, use File › Save to your computer. When a change breaks everything, going back costs one click.

#Milestone 1: The skeleton

Before any jumping, make the game flow. You need two backdrops (Title, with the game name and controls written on it, and Cave), and these variables and lists, all For all sprites:

  • Variables: state, level, lives, level name.
  • Lists: level names, start x, start y, crystal x, crystal y, bat count, bat speed.

This is the whole Stage. It runs the title, loops through the levels, and picks an ending:

The n key is a test shortcut that finishes the current level instantly. With it you can check the whole flow now, and later jump straight to level 3 without replaying levels 1 and 2. (Delete it, or keep it as a secret, before you share.)

Done when: the green flag shows the title, space starts the game, the level name monitor reads The Cellar, pressing n moves to The Mines and then The Summit, and a third n ends the game (silently for now, since nothing answers you win yet). Right-click the level name monitor and choose large readout so it looks like part of the game.

#Milestone 2: The player and one level

Bring in Level and Pip from Crystal Climb. If you're signed in, drag them across with the Backpack at the bottom of the editor; offline, right-click each sprite and choose export, then use Upload Sprite in the new project. Paint Level costume 1 as The Cellar. The Level sprite needs one new script:

Pip's movement moves from the green flag to begin play, and placing Pip moves to load level. A respawn custom block keeps both in step:

fix vertical is the Module 6 Practice block; tick Run without screen refresh for it, and leave respawn unticked (it has nothing to hurry). Add the Jump and Bonk sounds from the sound library first. touching (Bat v)? is always false until Milestone 4 adds bats, so it's safe to include now.

Done when: Pip walks, jumps, and lands cleanly on The Cellar, falling into a pit costs a life and returns Pip to the start, and losing all 5 lives ends the game.

#Milestone 3: Goals and three levels

The Crystal ends each level. It moves into place during load level and starts watching during begin play:

Setting state is all the Crystal does. The Stage's wait until notices, and the next pass of its loop loads the next level. Now paint Level costumes 2 and 3, and adjust the start and crystal numbers in set up game to fit your layouts.

Done when: you can play all three levels in order without the n key, every level starts with Pip standing in open air, and the crystal is reachable on each one.

#Milestone 4: Bats, clones, and a custom block

Add the library sprite Bat at size 40. The original hides and spawns; the clones fly.

Make speed For this sprite only. Three decisions are worth noticing:

  • delete this clone on load level clears last level's bats. The original ignores that block, so it survives to spawn again.
  • Bats spawn on begin play, not load level, because by then Pip is already at its start point and distance to (Pip v) measures the right spot.
  • spawn bat keeps trying random spots until it finds one at least 150 steps from Pip, so no bat appears on top of the player. Tick Run without screen refresh for it so the search finishes in one frame.

Done when: each level has the right number of bats (1, 2, then 4), they flap and bounce around, touching one costs a life, and no bat from an earlier level is ever left behind.

#Milestone 5: Difficulty that rises and adapts

The rising part is already in your lists: more bats on later levels. Check the curve by playing it. If The Summit is a wall, lower its bat count or bat speed in set up game, not in the bat scripts.

For the adaptive part, use the helping hand from Module 7's Practice. Paint Level costumes 4 to 6 as copies of 1 to 3, each with one extra platform that makes the hardest jump easier, away from the start point. Make a falls here variable, set it to 0 in Pip's load level script, and add this inside Pip's life-loss if, after change [lives v] by (-1):

The Level sprite answers:

Done when: three falls on any level makes the helper platform appear, and moving to the next level removes it.

#Milestone 6: Feedback, instructions, and endings

The game works; now make it talk. Pip announces the endings:

Then work through this list: controls written on the Title backdrop, the lives and level name monitors placed where they don't cover platforms, a sound for every action (jump, bonk, collect), and the crystal's two costumes animating so it catches the eye.

Done when: a friend who has never seen the game can start it, understand the goal, and reach an ending without you saying a word. You'll test exactly that in the next lesson.

#Translating the skeleton to your game

Skeleton part Ghost Patrol: Siege Lantern Dive Spell Duel
level wave number cave depth opponent number
Level costume backdrop per wave cave walls per depth opponent's arena
Crystal sets level done Stage sees ghosts left reach 0 pearls left reaches 0 opponent's power reaches 0
Bat clones ghost clones pearl and jellyfish clones spell particle clones
Lists per level wave size, spawn gap pearls, air time, jellyfish question range, opponent power
Adaptive part ghost speed bonus extra air after a failed dive question range adapts

Check your understanding

2 questions

1Why do the bats spawn on begin play instead of load level?

  • Clones can be made from any script.

  • During load level, Pip might still be standing where the last level ended.

  • It's the opposite: by begin play, the costume has already changed.

Show answer

B. During load level, Pip might still be standing where the last level ended.

2What does the n key script let you do?

  • Finishing a level instantly makes the flow testable from Milestone 1.

  • It only works while state is playing.

  • It sets state; it doesn't touch lives.

Show answer

A. Finishing a level instantly makes the flow testable from Milestone 1.

Key takeaways

  • Build the flow first: title, levels, endings. Then fill in the gameplay.
  • Every milestone ends playable, tested, and saved as its own version.
  • load level gets everything into place; begin play starts things moving.
  • delete this clone at the top of a load level receiver clears old clones and leaves the original alone.
  • Tune difficulty in the level data, not inside the scripts.

#Further reading

  • Backpack on the Scratch Wiki (opens in a new tab): how to carry sprites and scripts between your projects.
  • Debugging Scripts on the Scratch Wiki (opens in a new tab): ways to find out what a misbehaving script is really doing.
